candidates.title: Equifinal pathways and subtypes: a developmental neuroimaging perspective on social differences in autism
candidates.abstract: Social differences are a defining feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Autistic individuals show differences across multiple domains of social processing, including reciprocal behavior, social communication, and interpretation of facial expressions (Bhat et al., 2022;Lord et al., 2000). While social behavior in autistic individuals differs from that of non-autistic peers, some of these differences may also be context-dependent and reflect adaptive strategies given underlying sensory and cognitive profiles (Grace et al., 2022). Various studies have probed the neural mechanisms underlying these differences. Self-and caregiver-report studies suggest differences in social motivation in autistic individuals (Marrus et al., 2024;Neuhaus et al., 2024), and neuroimaging evidence implicates reward-related regions such as the ACC, vmPFC, OFC, amygdala, insula, and striatum (Clements et al., 2018). An alternative view emphasizes differences in understanding others' perspectives, associated with the mentalizing/Theory of Mind processes (Kanske, 2018), including medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), temporoparietal junction, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Abu Hoof et al., 2025;Jayashankar et al., 2023). Additionally, co-existing hyper-and hypoconnectivity in social brain regions (Yi et al., 2022) point to the roles of developmental timing and the specificity of certain brain regions in influencing connectivity patterns in ASD (Uddin et al., 2013). This lack of generalizability reveals the biological and behavioral complexity of ASD (King et al., 2019). To reconcile these co-existing hypotheses, our opinion article introduces a two-dimensional framework-comprising functional operations and developmental spatiotemporal specificity-by selectively synthesizing evidence primarily from MRI studies published over the past decade. We suggest that these mixed empirical findings may stem from the intrinsic heterogeneity of ASD, which gives rise to multiple potential developmental pathways. Consequently, ostensibly similar social differences in ASD may represent a common behavioral outcome arising from distinct developmental alterations that progressively shape specialized brain networks.Within our two-dimensional framework (Fig. 1), the first dimension focuses on functional operations, investigating whether autistic individuals exhibit atypical neural responses for distinct components of social processing and other basic processes that shape social behavior. The social motivation hypothesis posits that autistic individuals show atypical patterns during social reward processing. A meta-analysis by Clements et al. (2018), based primarily on autistic males from childhood to adulthood without intellectual disability, reported reduced striatal responses to social and non-social rewards. However, a systematic review across multiple measures found the evidence for this hypothesis to be mixed, as reward-related differences vary by reward type, task, and brain region (Bottini, 2018). Alternatively, the mentalizing differences hypothesis proposes that social differences primarily stem from alterations in mentalizing abilities, supported by task-based evidence including only male adults (Chen et al., 2023). However, a large cross-sectional sample spanning childhood to adulthood reveals that IQ-matched autistic males and females exhibit distinct mentalizing-network restingstate connectivity, with temporoparietal hyperconnectivity in males but medial prefrontal and precuneus hypoconnectivity in females (Yang & Lee, 2018). Beyond these specifically social processes, a review integrating behavioral, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging evidence argues that atypicalities in other cognitive functions, such as motor planning and predictive control can also contribute to social differences in ASD (Casartelli et al., 2016). These foundational alterations may lead to differences in action understanding and social initiation (Casartelli et al., 2016;Kilroy et al., 2022;Stillesjö et al., 2025). Together, these findings show how atypicalities in partially distinct functional operations-reward, mentalizing, motor prediction as illustrative examples-can each manifest as social differences.The second dimension maps neurodevelopmental trajectories, examining how social phenotypes in ASD link to specific developmental windows and brain regions. Prenatally, certain types of ASD risk genes were found converging in deep-layer projection neurons of the prefrontal and motor cortices across both sexes via post-mortem analysis (Willsey et al., 2013), suggesting early vulnerability of local regions, though this does not rule out alterations in other brain regions. Structural studies of high-familial-risk infant cohorts show that, during the first year, infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis exhibit hyperexpansion of cortical surface area (Hazlett et al., 2017). These systemic alterations in perceptual, attentional, motor, and social domains often emerge before overt ASD behavioral traits manifest (Elsabbagh & Johnson, 2016). In the second year and beyond, overall brain volume overgrowth was detected, correlating with the severity of later social differences (Hazlett et al., 2017;Piven et al., 2017). Together, current findings suggest that neurodevelopmental alterations unfold across multiple developmental stages. This developmental perspective also provides a time window for interpreting the functional alterations described in the first dimension. For autistic children, resting-state evidence shows attenuated effective connectivity between the mPFC and amygdala, which are nodes shared by the mentalizing and reward networks (Li et al., 2021). By early adolescence, task-based interactive social reward elicited comparable striatal and temporoparietal responses across autistic and neurotypical groups (McNaughton et al., 2023), so neither reward-nor mentalizing-related regions showed differences in this paradigm. In autistic adults, social differences may also involve multimodal structural and functional atypicalities within the fusiform gyrus, mPFC, and amygdala (Sato & Uono, 2019). These regions are components of the 'social brain', which support processes including reward anticipation and mentalizing (Frith, 2007). Beyond these specialized circuits, multimodal evidence links autistic social differences to alterations across widespread networks (Müller & Fishman, 2018) and reduced global efficiency in the white matter connectome (Cai et al., 2022). Across these developmental stages, we propose one possible pattern-both global and localized brain alterations may coexist in early life, with atypicalities gradually emerging in higher-level functional networks as social function develops with age. However, the dominant imaging modality differs across age, so developmental shifts remain partly confounded with method. Cross-study comparisons are further limited by methodological variability-task design, head motion, medication, and scanner effects-and by the largely cross-sectional design, with longitudinal data in infancy coming from high-familial-risk cohorts whose findings may not extend to the broader autistic population. Participant samples also rarely include individuals with intellectual disability, and sex shapes mentalizing-network alterations (Yang & Lee, 2018). Such variations, however, are unlikely to fully explain the inconsistencies. The remainder points to genuine within-diagnosis heterogeneity.From heterogeneity to equifinality: rethinking social differences in ASD Our framework illustrates how heterogeneity-the biological diversity within ASD-leads to equifinality, where different developmental pathways converge onto a similar, clinically defined social phenotype. One possible explanation for the inconsistencies is the etiological heterogeneity within autistic populations (Müller & Fishman, 2018;Parellada et al., 2014). For instance, Rødgaard et al. (2019) observed a longitudinal decrease in differences between autistic and neurotypical participants from 1966 to 2019. This narrowing partly indicates broadening diagnostic criteria and highlights heterogeneity within ASD. Our framework aligns with the evidence that diverse etiological mechanisms can lead to generalized ASD traits (Fenning et al., 2019;Qi et al., 2020). This equifinality explains why heterogeneity is a barrier to understanding social differences in ASD, as a single clinical diagnosis often masks highly diverse biological pathways. Several hypotheses investigate why ASD shows this equifinality in social differences. Johnson (2017) proposed that some autistic behaviors may reflect early-life adaptation to atypical neural signal processing. For example, social withdrawal may serve as an adaptive strategy to limit sensory and cognitive input when the brain shows atypicalities in handling multidimensional, parallel, and dynamic social stimuli. On this account, the social brain network's high metabolic demand and reliance on long-range integration may render it particularly vulnerable to subtle synaptic alterations. Because such adaptation depends on compensation, environment, and learning, similar early alterations need not lead to the same outcome; the framework thus describes probabilistic rather than fixed developmental routes. Additionally, the cascade hypothesis suggests that the foundational alterations may result in missed critical social learning opportunities. For example, infants' reduced object manipulation may limit the caregiver's language input, while atypical sensory attention can affect social cue recognition. Consequently, these initial disruptions may lead to social differences (Bradshaw et al., 2022;Iverson et al., 2023). If diverse pathways converge on similar social outcomes, the research task becomes to delineate these distinct pathways-that is, to identify meaningful biological subtypes. Our framework makes a further prediction: autistic individuals matched on similar socialcommunication profiles are predicted to show distinguishable longitudinal network trajectories. Classifying more homogeneous subgroups within ASD may address this heterogeneity (Harris, 2019;Rødgaard et al., 2019). For example, Litman et al. (2025) identified four geneticdevelopmental subtypes. These subtypes-moderate challenges, broadly affected, social or behavioral, and mixed ASD with developmental delay-correlated with specific sets of genetic alterations acting at variable developmental windows (prenatal to adolescence). In terms of brain networks, Lombardo et al. (2019) identified a subtype that features early visual-social engagement differences, associated with hypoconnectivity between the default mode network and occipitotemporal cortex. At the micro-level, subtype-specific gene sets are linked to different molecular signaling pathways, involving immune and synapse function, G-protein-coupled receptor signaling, and protein synthesis (Buch et al., 2023). Taken together, while these criteria of classification vary, they may not be mutually exclusive. In fact, this evidence depicts several potential links on how developmental timing, as well as genetic or neural pathways shape ASD phenotypes.Our framework locates social differences in ASD within interacting networks that develop over time, rather than in fixed core regions. We propose that social differences should be viewed as the convergent outcome of various alterations across a wide range of neural networks. Importantly, the so-called social brain is increasingly viewed as an interconnected 'social connectome' including cooperating and overlapping networks (Maliske et al., 2023;Maliske & Kanske, 2022;Schurz et al., 2020). Because social cognition draws on brain regions involved in perception, motor skills, and attention (Van Overwalle, 2009), alterations in these foundational levels can cascade upward to social differences (Iverson et al., 2023). Unlike models that describe how these alterations arise or spread, our framework maps where to look for them-at which developmental stage and in which operation. Future work should consider developmental timing to explore whether these atypical developments are due to prenatal or genetic factors, or to the cascading effects of synaptic pruning. In addition, rather than focusing solely on one mechanism that fits the broad ASD criteria defined by behavioral traits, future studies should emphasize identifying subtypes characterized by divergent neural developmental trajectories. Indeed, recent advances have identified distinct ASD subtypes based on brain connectivity patterns and developmental timing (Litman et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2025;Qiao et al., 2025). However, valid ASD subtypes should reflect coherent neurodevelopmental pathways rather than mere statistical clusters, which are sensitive to analytical choices. More fundamentally, whether heterogeneity is discrete or continuous remains an open question for future research. Ideally, these pathways should exhibit longitudinal stability and neurobiological coherence across developmental trajectories and show external clinical validity, including the ability to predict behavioral profiles and intervention response. Understanding the neurodevelopmental evolution of these subtypes could then enhance the interpretability and replicability of studies and guide precise interventions (Kamp-Becker et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2025). Such subtyping efforts may facilitate more tailored interventions for specific autistic subgroups. For instance, preliminary evidence suggests that some autistic individuals with reward-network alterations may benefit from interventions targeting social reward processing (Baker et al., 2020), although whether reward-network-defined subtypes predict treatment response remains to be established. Developmental timing is also critical, as evidence supports the importance of early intervention during periods of heightened neuroplasticity (Bradshaw et al., 2022;Iverson et al., 2023;Nelson et al., 2024), despite limited evidence for imaging-defined subtype-specific early interventions. Finally, because social differences can emerge as an adaptive response to reduce cognitive load (Johnson, 2017), interventions should be carefully evaluated for potential anxiety, distress, or other unintended effects, given concerns about incomplete adverse-event reporting (Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021). Therefore, interventions should support sensory and cognitive mechanisms while also considering an autistic individual's support level. For now, our framework guides future stratification research rather than clinical decision-making. To sum up, we argue that embracing equifinality and mapping functional operations onto developmental spatiotemporal trajectories can enable biologically grounded subtyping and, ultimately, more humane, individualized support that prioritizes autonomy and quality of life over the normalization of social behavior. mentalizing/theory of mind (blue), and motor prediction and other cognitive functions (coral); green marks regions where the social motivation and mentalizing/theory of mind operations overlap. Solid outlines denote supported findings; the dashed cell denotes a non-confirmatory finding (no group difference). Prenatal-infancy alterations are not functionally specific and are therefore placed below the functional axis rather than assigned to a single operation. candidates.title: How large language models judge and influence human cooperation
candidates.abstract: Humans increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to support decisions in social settings. Previous work suggests that such tools can shape people's moral judgments. However, how LLMs evaluate decisions in social dilemmas, and the long-term implications of LLM-based assessments on human cooperation-driven by indirect reciprocity, reputations, and the capacity to judge interactions of others-remain unclear. We evaluate the social norms of 21 state-of-the-art LLMs when judging more than 40,000 fictitious decisions in social dilemmas. Through an evolutionary game-theoretical model, we study prosociality in populations adhering to these norms, theoretically studying their potential impact on long-term human cooperation. We observe a remarkable agreement in LLMs when evaluating actions against opponents perceived as good. Yet, there is large within- and between-model variance when assessing actions toward ill-reputed individuals. Our theoretical analysis reveals that these differences can significantly impact the prevalence of cooperation within our model. Finally, we show that prompt-based interventions can steer LLM norms, particularly when these define objective goals. Our theoretical model links LLM-based advice to long-term social dynamics, highlighting the importance of designing LLM norms considering their potential effects on human cooperation.

candidates.title: Empathic Concern for Violators Modulates Victims' Evaluation of Third-Party Punishment Outcomes: Behavioral and EEG Evidence
candidates.abstract: When fairness conflicts with empathy-induced altruism, victims often reduce punishment to protect violators' welfare. Whether this influence extends to outcome evaluations when punishment is implemented by third parties remains unclear. We combined an adapted Third-Party Dictator Game with electroencephalography (EEG) to address this. Participants received unfair allocations from violators and evaluated third-party punishment (TPP) outcomes. Empathic concern was induced by portraying violators as being in need. Behaviorally, victims in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition rated no-punishment and partial-punishment outcomes as more appropriate but complete-punishment outcomes as less appropriate. Partial-punishment outcomes received the highest ratings in the empathy condition, reflecting a balance between protecting violators' welfare and restoring fairness. Neurally, partial-punishment outcomes induced smaller P2 amplitudes in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition, suggesting lower motivational salience because they better matched victims' goals. No-punishment outcomes induced larger LPP amplitudes in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition, reflecting sustained processing of their affective and motivational significance. Parietal alpha suppression was weaker in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition, indicating reduced sustained attention to TPP outcomes. Together, these findings suggest that empathic concern shapes victims' evaluations of third-party norm-enforcement outcomes, extending its influence beyond contexts in which the empathizing individual also implements punishment.

candidates.title: From Self to Others? Testing Whether Brief Mindfulness Reduces Intergroup Bias through Decentering or Self-Compassion
candidates.abstract: AbstractBrief mindfulness reliably changes how individuals relate to their own internal experiences, but whether these intrapersonal changes generalize to intergroup responding remains unclear. This preregistered experiment (N = 91) examined whether mindfulness-related processes—decentering and compassionate self-responding—were associated with socio-affective responses toward in-group and out-group members. Participants completed an adapted Socio-affective Video Task using AI-generated images to assess compassion, personal distress, and prosocial giving. Brief mindfulness was significantly linked to increased decentering and compassionate self-responding. Contrary to preregistered hypotheses, the intervention did not reduce intergroup bias in compassion, personal distress, or the empathic Dictator Game. Findings suggest that brief mindfulness primarily influences proximal intrapersonal processes, whereas changes in intergroup socio-affective responding may be limited.

candidates.title: The Structure of Social Cognition: Precursors, Mechanisms, and Competencies
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Social competence is an architecture rather than a unitary capacity, and the cognitive science of social behaviour remains fragmentedacross disciplines that do not always share a vocabulary. We propose a three-level decomposition, drawing on cognitive science,developmental psychology, philosophy of mind, psycholinguistics, social ethology and AI research. Seven candidate socio-cognitiveprecursors (embodied, pre-representational dispositions such as animacy detection, gaze following and emotional contagion) sitbelow seven socio-cognitive mechanisms (goal inference, mentalizing, mutual modelling, shared intentionality, meta-cognitive socialmodelling, norm representation, reciprocity tracking), which compose into thirty-eight domain competencies. The mechanisms areindividuated by dissociability and ordered by their dependencies, with the evidence stated for each boundary. That ordering carriesour main structural claim: goal inference, not mentalizing, is the foundational mechanism, and coordination, joint commitment andcommon ground (short of its epistemic form) do not require belief attribution. This departs from the theory-of-mind-centred accountsthe field has organised itself around. We also discuss two factors that are not specific to social cognition, yet play a fundamental role init: situatedness, and central coherence, which we argue is a parameter on belief inference rather than a socio-cognitive mechanismper-se. Finally, we compile a catalogue of experimental paradigms, including matched “fine-cuts” task pairs that separate surface socialperformance from socio-cognitive competence, and set out how the framework could be tested by socio-cognitive ablation.

candidates.title: Developing a Mealtime Assistance Framework for Geriatric Psychiatric Inpatients: A Narrative Review
candidates.abstract: IntroductionMalnutrition is highly prevalent amongst psychiatric inpatients, with prevalence reaching up to 42.5%. Geriatric-psychiatric inpatients, in particular, face complex nutritional barriers distinct from typical hospital malnutrition. To date, there is limited guidance on adapting mealtime assistance strategies to the complex needs of geriatric-psychiatric inpatients.MethodsA systematized narrative review aligned with SANRA was conducted to develop a mealtime assistance framework. Personal and institutional challenges in geriatric-psychiatric care were identified, followed by a review of successful mealtime practices from various inpatient settings, and then key elements were modified to fit the unique needs of the target population.ResultsPersonal challenges to addressing malnutrition in geriatric psychiatric care include medication-induced appetite and taste changes, apathy, low motivation, and altered circadian rhythm patterns. Institutional barriers include overly rigid organizational approaches, deficits in staff knowledge relating to evidence-based nutrition, competing staff priorities and a predominant focus on pharmacotherapy, which may cause approaches to physical health and nutritional status to be inadequate. Key nutritional interventions from the literature include improving the mealtime environment through protected mealtimes and auditory optimization, enhancing human interaction between staff and patients, implementing a 'train-the-trainer' model, and using oral nutritional supplements and food fortification. Key adaptations to address specific challenges in this population include flexible mealtime scheduling to accommodate disrupted routines, specialized staff training in patient empathy and mutual reciprocity, and the use of sealed packaging for oral nutrition supplements to address paranoia.ConclusionImplementing mealtime interventions tailored explicitly to the geriatric psychiatric inpatient population is vital for addressing malnutrition and improving both physical and mental health outcomes. This review provides a novel, setting-specific mealtime assistance framework for this uniquely vulnerable population, making testing and cost-effectiveness analysis an important priority for future research.

candidates.title: Indigenous Marriage Counselling as a Psychosocial System: Cultural Practices, Psychological Mechanisms and Marital Regulation in South Sudan
candidates.abstract: Marriage in South Sudan operates simultaneously as an intimate partnership, a kinship arrangement and a community institution. This article examines indigenous marriage counselling as a psychosocial system rather than as a collection of isolated customs. Drawing primarily on the first two objectives of a doctoral study—identifying traditional marriage counselling practices and the psychological principles embedded within them—the paper analyses how elders’ guidance, family participation, cultural instruction, mediation and reconciliation function as mechanisms of behavioural learning, emotional regulation, social accountability and relational repair. The underlying study employed a mixed-methods descriptive cross-sectional design. Of 250 questionnaires distributed, 242 were returned (96.8%). The six-item traditional counselling scale produced a mean of 4.30 (SD=0.79; Cronbach’s α=.849). Traditional leaders’ role in resolving marital conflicts received the strongest endorsement (M=4.48), while all six items recorded at least 84% agreement or strong agreement. Open-ended responses identified respect, communication, trust, cooperation, elders, family support and cultural or religious values as recurrent resources for successful marriage. The analysis interprets these practices through Family Systems Theory, Social Learning Theory, Attachment Theory, Cognitive Behavioural Theory and Ecological Systems Theory. The findings suggest that indigenous counselling can be understood as a layered psychosocial regulatory system: it teaches marital norms, creates culturally legitimate spaces for dialogue, mobilises support networks, reinforces accountability, and facilitates reconciliation. However, these strengths do not justify uncritical preservation. Risks involving confidentiality, unequal authority, coercion, violence and complex psychological problems require safeguarding and professional referral. The article concludes that culturally responsive marriage counselling in South Sudan should preserve beneficial indigenous mechanisms while distinguishing community guidance from professional psychological treatment and high-risk safeguarding functions.

candidates.title: Modulation of vicarious fear extinction with oxytocin in social anxiety disorder
candidates.abstract: Abstract Approximately half of patients with social anxiety disorder (SAD) do not achieve remission from cognitive behavioral therapy, which relies on direct extinction of social fears. Direct extinction can be inefficient and costly; social learning theories propose that social fears may be extinguished vicariously through others’ safety experiences. Potentiating vicarious extinction through pharmacologic agents such as oxytocin, an endogenous neuromodulator involved in social affiliation and fear regulation, may offer a novel strategy for augmenting extinction in SAD. We hypothesized that vicarious extinction would reduce conditioned threat responses in SAD, oxytocin would potentiate the effects of vicarious extinction, and oxytocin’s effects would be moderated by gender. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, participants ( n = 104; n = 51 SAD, n = 53 healthy controls) first completed an acquisition procedure outside of the scanner, and received 24 IU intranasal oxytocin or matching placebo prior to completing a vicarious extinction and reinstatement test while undergoing fMRI and recording skin conductance responses (SCR). During acquisition, there was a significant main effect of stimulus type, as all participants displayed greater SCR in CS+s compared to CS-, suggesting that the task was effective in evoking conditioned threat. SCR findings partially supported a pattern of attenuated conditioned threat responses to the vicariously extinguished cue (CS + S) compared to the unextinguished cue (CS + R), but there remained a significant difference between the CS + S and CS-, and this was evident across all participants, not just in SAD. fMRI results did not reveal benefits of vicarious extinction in SAD. Contrary to hypotheses, there were no effects of diagnostic group or drug condition or their interaction; oxytocin showed no effects on SCRs or brain responses to CS + R versus CS + S cues. However, as expected, oxytocin demonstrated gender-dependent effects, as fMRI results showed significant drug by gender interactions in the amygdala, insula, hippocampus, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, with oxytocin increasing threat responding to vicariously non-extinguished CS+ in men compared to women. Findings underscore effects of oxytocin that vary by gender in fear regulation-related neural circuitry.

candidates.title: From Preference to Reciprocity: Decentralized Matching with Empirically Grounded LLM-agent Based Modeling
candidates.abstract: Bipartite matching is a fundamental problem in game theory and market design. Classical approaches such as Gale--Shapley assume complete preferences and centralized computation, whereas many real-world matching processes are decentralized, asynchronous, and shaped by sequential interaction under limited information. We propose a dynamic bipartite matching framework that combines large language model (LLM) agents with contextual bandits. In a simulated Chinese marriage market, economically grounded LLM agents evaluate locally encountered candidates, while agent-specific Logistic-UCB models learn reciprocal acceptance from realized proposal outcomes. The mechanism therefore separates two decisions---\emph{whom do I like?} and \emph{who is likely to like me back?}---without requiring ex ante market-wide preference rankings. We first validate LLM-induced mate preferences against the empirical conditional-logit reference across multiple LLM backbones. In the $50\times50$ matching experiment, Bandit-UCB achieves the highest mean mutual welfare (56.01 versus 54.87 for Gale--Shapley), a smaller gender rank gap than the classical baselines, and the fewest blocking pairs among the LLM-ABM policies. Learned acceptance models show economically interpretable gender-differentiated associations, while counterfactual setups reveal no systematic unilateral advantage from prior search knowledge. Overall, these results support the advantages of decentralized matching with LLM-based behavioral modeling and online learning under incomplete information for economic simulation and computational social science research.

candidates.title: Contextual Interpersonal Calibration (CIC): An Iterative Method for Autistic Adults Decoding Implicit Communicative Codes in Neurotypical-Dominant Environments
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Contextual Interpersonal Calibration (CIC) is a method for autistic adults decoding implicit communicative codes in neurotypical-majority environments, formalized here as an explicit, iterative alternative to communicative intuition. The method proceeds through a recursive cycle of observation, local hypothesis, register selection, and falsification, tracked across six operational variables including cognitive cost. CIC positions itself relative to Communication Accommodation Theory, single-case ABAB experimental design, and Bayesian models of social inference, combining elements of each into a procedure usable in real time without training in any of the three fields. The method functions as a bridge rather than a permanent adaptation: it represents only the autistic person's half of a relational approach, with reciprocity from the interlocutor tracked as a variable subject to the same falsification discipline as any other hypothesis. CIC is presented as an operational proposal grounded in nearly fifty years of the author's own recursive practice; the literature cited documents the communicative problem it responds to and the theoretical precedents the procedure draws on, rather than validating the procedure's own efficacy.

candidates.title: A risk-based view of trust in human–machine collaboration on cooking robots
candidates.abstract: Human–machine collaboration is becoming increasingly prevalent across a wide range of industries. However, the risks associated with the adoption of emerging technologies have triggered a crisis of trust, leading to widespread concerns about the deployment of collaborative machines in the service industry. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the role of trust in human–machine collaboration from a risk-based view, with the following research objectives: (1) to identify the antecedents of trust and test hypothesized associations among trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, and use behavior; and (2) to construct a risk-based model capturing the associations of trust with behavior in human–machine collaboration. Survey data were collected from 201 respondents in China and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that empathy, competence, reciprocity, and assurance were associated with trust in collaborative machines, while perceived risk mediates the hypothesized paths between trust and adoption intention. These findings provide insights into designing for trust in human–machine collaboration on cooking robots.

candidates.title: Appendices A-E: Bias in AI Video Interview Evaluations: Effects of Autistic-Associated Behaviors and Debiasing Procedures
candidates.abstract: Adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience employment disparities despite evidence that they possess strengths valued in the workplace. One barrier is the interview, where interviewer impressions are often formed from non-verbal behavioral cues. Differences in these behaviors are common in ASD and contribute to negative evaluations. While the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in hiring practices is rapidly increasing, it remains unclear whether these behaviors bring out inherent biases within these systems. The current study examines whether AI Large Language Models (LLM) assign lower evaluative ratings to candidates displaying autistic-associated behaviors and whether a debiasing procedure can reduce these effects. Three AI LLM models rated candidates in mock interview clips across four conditions: control (neurotypical behavior), limited eye contact, monotone speech, and low conversational reciprocity. The AI LLM rated the candidate on interpersonal and cognitive attributes and overall hireability before and after being exposed to pro-neurodiversity research. The LLMs assigned lower ratings in all non-control conditions. After the debiasing procedure, ratings increased across conditions. These findings suggest that AI LLM systems may replicate bias toward neurodivergent applicants but also suggest that these biases can be mitigated.

candidates.title: THE ASYLUM : Disruptive Cognitive Operations and Inner Ecology
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Disruptive Cognitive Operations and Inner Ecology Action-Research Lessons Learned from a Dis|mis Administrative Incident This book is an action-research study of lessons learned from a dis|mis administrative incident. It uses the incident as a situated case through which to examine how administrative uncertainty, informational asymmetry, technological mediation, institutional inertia, and contested interpretation can affect cognition, expression, dignity, and public trust. The project is guided by the attached work’s progression from “Fundamental Rights At Risk” and “On Partiality” to “On Liberty of Thinking,” “On Inner Peace & Recensions,” “Introducing CogOps,” “On Cognitive Health,” and the case studies on judicial impartiality, private affiliations, oath conflict, and SIS–Schengen transparency. The table of contents therefore provides the project’s conceptual route: from rights and institutional balance, through cognition and inner life, towards administrative, technological, and governance risks. The research does not present the personal account as conclusive proof of intentional wrongdoing. Rather, it treats the incident as a source of lessons learned, research questions, provisional concepts, and methodological warnings. The purpose is to distinguish observed events from interpretation, allegation, metaphor, and hypothesis while asking how comparable vulnerabilities might arise in other administrative environments. From rights to cognition The first part of the research begins with fundamental rights and institutional impartiality. In the chapter “On Partiality,” the attached work states: “It is also relational: whenever you are judged, a relationship is involved.” This proposition provides an important starting point for action research. An administrative decision is not only a technical act; it occurs within a relationship involving a citizen, a public agent, an institution, a body of law, and a surrounding informational environment. A failure of communication, an absence of reasons, a delay, or an inability to challenge a decision can therefore produce effects extending beyond the immediate administrative matter. The same chapter gives a second guiding image: “We are all equal under gravity.” Here, the balance functions as a non-technical symbol of equality, impartiality, and the need to prevent power from becoming detached from rights. Within the proposed research, this image is translated into questions about procedural fairness, equal access to information, the visibility of relevant affiliations, and the ability of affected persons to participate meaningfully in decisions concerning them. Liberty of thinking The chapter “On Liberty of Thinking” provides the closest conceptual foundation for the study of inner ecology. It describes writing and symbolic expression as a means of creating distance from an overwhelming or difficult experience: “Being able to formulate, express, and work on things symbolically helps us create emotional distance.” This observation is central to the action-research design. Recension, writing, drawing, multilingual expression, and documentary reconstruction are not treated merely as literary devices. They are used as practical research instruments through which an individual experience can be reviewed, organised, questioned, and made accessible to others. The chapter also describes expression as a form of shelter: “It was therefore a genuine shelter to be able to express ourselves through this ‘way of the pencil.’” Adapted to a CERREV-oriented research programme, this becomes a question about the conditions under which citizens and public agents can formulate disagreement without escalation. The research therefore examines whether accessible forms of expression can reduce informational dissonance, support self-correction, and create a more reliable basis for institutional dialogue. Inner peace and recension The chapter “On Inner Peace & Recensions” defines the inner domain broadly, including: “our inner condition; our constitution; our state; our personal ecology; our psychology; our cognition.” This passage directly informs the use of inner ecology in the present research. Inner ecology refers to the personal and collective conditions in which attention, memory, language, emotion, embodiment, creativity, and judgement interact. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not presume decline. It is an analytical concept for studying how cognitive and relational environments may be supported or disrupted. The chapter further describes recension as a way to improve accessibility: “What was inaccessible at the beginning became an opening towards accessibility through recension.” This principle gives the action-research project a practical orientation. The researcher’s task is not only to describe an incident but also to make its relevant lessons more accessible to public agents, researchers, citizens, and communities. This requires plain language, transparent sourcing, multilingual sensitivity, and a clear separation between what is known, what is inferred, and what remains uncertain. Introducing CogOps The chapter “Introducing CogOps” extends the inquiry from individual cognition to informational and commercial environments. It identifies influence mechanisms such as reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, scarcity, and perceived value, and concludes with the practical instruction: “Learn to say no. Resist these logics. Use discernment.” For the proposed research, disruptive cognitive operations are therefore not limited to military or security contexts. The term is used more broadly and cautiously to describe processes that shape attention, interpretation, consent, judgement, or behaviour. These processes may be commercial, administrative, technological, social, cultural, or accidental. The research will examine how such operations can arise through: persuasive or emotionally charged communication; repeated narratives and social conformity; informational overload; inaccessible or opaque procedures; algorithmic or platform-based mediation; technological dependence and vendor lock-in; unequal access to language, documentation, or professional assistance; and the inability of institutions to reproduce or explain their own decisions. The term remains a research hypothesis rather than a conclusion about the incident. Its value lies in helping identify mechanisms that can be tested against documents, timelines, comparable cases, and institutional procedures. Cognitive health and technological mediation The chapter “On Cognitive Health” describes the risk that digital environments may maximise the use of: “our brains; time; attention; and emotional energy.” This concern links the personal incident to a broader study of technological mediation. Public administration increasingly depends on digital forms, search systems, databases, platforms, automated classification, and privately developed software. These tools can improve access and efficiency, but they can also introduce opacity, dependency, unequal usability, and new forms of cognitive load. The chapter “On Freedom of Consciousness & Intellectual Property” calls attention to the use of privately owned creative tools in public contexts and asks whether dependence on such tools can narrow independent creativity. It states: “Creative freedom requires room to experiment.” This idea can guide a CERREV research question concerning technological vulnerability: whether public agents and citizens retain sufficient control to inspect, adapt, replace, and contest the tools through which administrative reality is produced. Administrative inertia and lessons learned The chapter “On Liberty of Thinking” introduces the term ADMINERTIA for a convergence of responsibility, accountability, culpability, and institutional hesitation. It asks whether an administrative agent can say: “I will take responsibility. I will get it written—not right, not wrong—so that this administrative inertia can escape a martial dead end.” This passage gives the project a direct action-research objective: to identify where an administrative process becomes difficult to explain, reproduce, challenge, or correct. The research will therefore document not only outcomes but also: what information was available at each stage; which actors had decision-making authority; how explanations were communicated; where delays or ambiguities appeared; whether the affected person could respond; which technological systems mediated the process; and how responsibility was allocated or obscured. The lesson learned is not that every administrative failure is deliberate. It is that unreproducible administration creates vulnerability, especially when citizens cannot determine what happened, why it happened, or how to seek correction. The central research question can therefore be formulated as follows: How can action-research lessons learned from a dis|mis administrative incident contribute to the study of disruptive cognitive operations and inner ecology within CERREV’s fields of risk and vulnerability research? Subsidiary questions are: How do administrative uncertainty and informational velocity affect the interpretation of a contested event? When does an ordinary technological or procedural shortcut become a source of structural vulnerability? How do partiality, opacity, resource scarcity, and institutional inertia affect dignity and public trust? Can recension, drawing, multilingual expression, local documentation, and human review support cognitive and administrative resilience? What safeguards can help institutions preserve impartiality, reproducibility, transparency, and freedom of thought?

candidates.title: From Shouting to Calm Conversations: A Qualitative Study of Family Communication Transformation Through a Culturally Adapted Multiple Family Group Therapy in HIV-Affected Families in Ghana
candidates.abstract: Family communication dysfunction significantly impacts HIV medication adherence and mental health outcomes among adolescents in sub-Saharan Africa, yet evidence-based family interventions remain scarce in resource-limited settings. This qualitative descriptive study examined family communication transformation following culturally adapted Multiple Family Group Therapy (MFGT) for adolescents living with HIV and their families in rural Ghana. Focus group discussions were conducted with 20 caregivers and 19 adolescents who completed the 11-session intervention. All core therapeutic content was delivered across sessions 1 through 10; the 11th session comprised a graduation ceremony and sustainability planning. Reflexive thematic analysis revealed four major themes: preintervention dysfunction (public shaming, adolescent defiance, spousal teknonymy, extended family triangulation); MFGT-facilitated skills (tone modulation, privacy-preserving correction, active listening); postintervention transformation (caregiver behavioral consolidation, adolescent reciprocal adaptation, spousal reconnection); and sustaining mechanisms (observational learning, metacognitive awareness, positive reinforcement, peer accountability). Communication improvements occurred bidirectionally, with caregiver changes catalyzing adolescent adaptations. Findings are theoretically interpreted through family systems theory, communication accommodation theory, social cognitive theory, and self-determination theory. Culturally adapted MFGT successfully transformed communication patterns while preserving traditional authority structures, suggesting potential for integration within HIV care systems in resource-limited settings.

candidates.title: When Positive Relational Experiences Backfire: Exposure to Forgiving, Consistently Trusting Agents Lowers Subsequent Reciprocity
candidates.abstract: Can exposure to a forgiving, consistently trusting partner improve interpersonal cooperation? Attachment theory suggests positive relational experiences can correct negative internal working models, but individuals high in rejection sensitivity (RS), characterized by anxious expectations of rejection, may be resistant to such corrective experiences due to stable negative expectations. We tested this using a randomized experiment (N = 206) in which participants played repeated trust games with HMM-based artificial agents that simulate human-like trust dynamics. After a baseline game, participants were exposed to either an idealized partner (an agent designed never to remain in a low-trust state, free from pre-programmed trust withdrawals, and consequently investing more; Manipulation) or a standard agent maintaining typical trust withdrawal patterns (Control), then played a final game with the standard agent; these features were varied together, so the design tests their joint effect. In the primary, powered contrast, exposure to the idealized partner reduced subsequent cooperation, and participants rated the unchanged post-exposure agent less favorably, a pattern consistent with a negative contrast effect, an interpretation developed after initial analysis. RS moderation was a planned analysis but was not separately powered: we detected no moderation of the reduction by RS, and an apparent RS difference in responsiveness to partner investment was not robust once participant-level variation in responsiveness was modeled. These findings suggest that brief exposure to an idealized partner does not universally promote cooperation and can reduce it, and point to expectation-updating, rather than exposure alone, as one candidate target for future interventions.

candidates.title: The Trust-Building Game: Dynamic Signaling, Markov Equilibrium, and Threshold Cooperation
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Trust in repeated interaction depends on how observed behavior changes future incentives as well as current responses. This paper develops a discounted dynamic Trust-Building Game in which a trust builder chooses observable binary signals, a public state aggregates past signals through a persistence-weighted recursion, and a trustee observes the updated state before deciding whether to cooperate. The trustee's cooperation cutoff is derived as a dynamic best response under stationary Markov strategies, while the builder's problem is characterized by a Bellman equation. We establish existence of a pure stationary Markov equilibrium, boundedness and monotonicity of the builder's value function, and exact bounds on the gain from positive signaling. These results identify a parameter regime in which the builder's unique optimal stationary policy has an activation-band structure: signaling is optimal only over an intermediate interval of public states, demonstrating that a monotone one-sided threshold policy cannot be imposed in general. We further derive the weighted-history representation of the public state, exact first-passage and cooperation times, finite-horizon cooperation fractions, geometric decay after signaling stops, and the minimum current signaling cost required to preserve cooperation for one period. Deterministic Bellman computations recover the analytically derived activation band without policy mismatches on the numerical grid and examine optimal signaling outside the analytically characterized regime. Additional computations verify the distinction between the threshold-state index and the first cooperative period and preserve cooperation at threshold equality. The framework is deliberately reduced form: the public state is neither a Bayesian posterior nor an empirically calibrated measure of psychological trust, and the numerical results are model evaluations rather than empirical evidence.

candidates.title: The neural architecture of social threat: A meta-analytic comparison of indirect and direct social threat.
candidates.abstract: Indirect and Direct Social Threat (IST and DST) are related but partially distinct forms of interpersonal adversity defined along two dimensions: threat perception, the explicitness and salience of harm, and behavioural reciprocity, the extent of bidirectional contingency and response opportunity. IST involves ambiguous or socially devaluing contexts with limited reciprocity, whereas DST entails overt hostility, clear antagonism, and reciprocal engagement. This distinction shows conceptual parallels with findings from rodent models of social interaction. We tested this framework using a coordinate-based Activation Likelihood Estimation (ALE) meta-analysis of human neuroimaging studies comprising 28 IST contrasts (N = 1081) and 28 DST contrasts (N = 855), with cluster-level family-wise error correction (p<.05). Findings were interpreted alongside passive and agonistic animal paradigms. Conjunction analysis identified shared spatial convergence in the left anterior insula (AI) extending into the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), consistent with salience-detection and regulatory processes. ALE contrast analysis showed stronger convergence for DST than IST in the right AI, bilateral claustrum, and anterior and mid-cingulate cortices, regions implicated in motivational salience and action preparation; no clusters emerged for IST relative to DST. Predicted IST-specific convergence in the temporoparietal junction and posterior cingulate cortex, and DST-related convergence in the amygdala and ventral striatum, were not observed. This pattern is conceptually consistent with animal evidence associating reciprocal threat with defensive readiness and action selection. Overall, findings partially support the framework: threat perception and behavioural reciprocity may help organise neural responses to social threat, while correspondence with passive-agonistic animal models remains provisional.

candidates.title: Assessing Individual Differences in Adult Theory of Mind Through Mental State Language: Human and Artificial Intelligence Approaches
candidates.abstract: Theory of mind is central to human social behavior, yet empirical studies rely largely on biased measures with limited ecological validity. We propose and evaluate the use of mental state language as a spontaneous indicator of theory of mind expressed in social interaction. Among research participants (334 undergraduate students, 63.8% non-Hispanic White, 74.3% female) engaged in a dyadic cooperative task with an unfamiliar peer, mental state language demonstrated strong convergent validity with established measures of theory of mind and, when compared to established measures, superior predictive validity for interpersonal functioning. Fine-tuned transformers and open-source generative large language models reliably replicated human coding of mental state language, enabling scalable assessment. These findings offer promising initial construct-validity evidence for mental state language as a measure of theory of mind, and motivate its extension to naturalistic, dynamically unfolding social interactions.

candidates.title: Contrast bias, not confirmation bias, shapes daily impression updating across social and non-social targets
candidates.abstract: Previous literature on impression updating has paid extensive attention to confirmation bias - the tendency to seek out, favour, interpret or remember information in a way that reinforces existing beliefs. Fewer studies examined the contrast effect/bias in the sequential updating of impressions. Contrast bias occurs when the difference between current beliefs and new information is exaggerated, leading to a stronger shift in evaluation than the new information alone would justify. In this work, we conducted two Ecological Momentary Experiments to capture real-world impression formation and updating on both social (e.g. an employee) and non-social (e.g. a vacation house) targets. We also developed novel computational models of biased impression updating based on parametric distortions of Bayesian ideal observers. Across the two studies, we found that daily impression updating exhibited significant contrast bias, with negative contrast bias exerting a stronger influence than positive ones. Additionally, we found no evidence for differences in impression updating between social and non-social targets. By focusing on within-person impression updating over time, these findings reveal contrast bias as a core dynamic of impression updating, systematically shaping how impressions change in response to inconsistent information.

candidates.title: Ego-R1: Agentic Chain-of-Tool-Thought for Ultra-Long Egocentric Video Reasoning
candidates.venue: IEEE Trans Pattern Anal Mach Intell
candidates.abstract: Egocentric videos are inherently long-form, as they provide a continuous, first-person perspective of daily life, capturing complex social interactions and routines that naturally span days or weeks. Understanding and reasoning over egocentric videos that span hours or even days poses significant challenges due to their length, multimodal nature, and complex temporal dependencies over long time horizons. To this end, we introduce Ego-R1, a novel framework for reasoning over ultra-long (i.e., days and weeks) egocentric videos. Ego-R1 leverages a structured Chain-of-Tool-Thought (CoTT) process, orchestrated by an Ego-R1 Agent trained via reinforcement learning (RL). Inspired by human problem-solving strategies, CoTT decomposes complex reasoning into modular steps, empowering the agent to act as a high-level controller that dynamically invokes specialized tools-such as hierarchical memory retrievers and multimodal perceptors-to iteratively and collaboratively answer sub-questions. This approach enables effective temporal abstraction, long-horizon dependency tracking, and step-by-step multimodal reasoning. The framework is built upon a flexible toolkit designed for efficient temporal retrieval and granular visual analysis: Hierarchical RAG (H-RAG), a text-based module that performs efficient top-down temporal localization by aggregating video logs from day-level summaries down to 10-minute intervals; Video-LLM, a short-horizon perception module that analyzes local temporal windows to interpret dynamic interactions; and VLM, a fine-grained vision-language model used to extract high-resolution details, such as text or object attributes, from specific frames. We design a two-stage training paradigm involving supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of a pretrained language model using CoTT data, to enable dynamic tool proposal for long-range reasoning; followed by RL, to enhance the performance of plan smartly with tools. To facilitate training, we construct Ego-R1 Data, which consists of Ego-CoTT-25 K for SFT and Ego-QA-4.4 K for RL. Furthermore, we evaluate Ego-R1 on a newly curated week-long video QA benchmark, Ego-R1 Bench, which contains hybrid-source, human-verified QA pairs. Extensive experiments show that our 3B-parameter Ego-R1 Agent achieves the strongest performance among open-weight and tool-agent baselines, while offering interpretable tool-grounded reasoning trajectories. On Ego-R1 Bench, Ego-R1 achieves 46.0% accuracy, substantially outperforming Gemini-1.5-Pro (38.3%) and LLaVA-Video (29.0%); we further report Gemini-3.1-Pro as a stronger closed-source reference at 53.7%. Moreover, the framework exhibits strong generalization to standard exocentric video benchmarks; by leveraging the long-video nature of egocentric data to train the orchestrator's planning capabilities rather than overfitting the perceptors to a specific view, our modular design remains robust across domains. Ego-R1 Agent achieves 64.9% accuracy on Video-MME (long), surpassing leading open-weight models. These results validate that dynamic, tool-augmented reasoning effectively bridges the gap between limited context windows and the demands of understanding both week-long first-person experiences and general long-form video content.

candidates.title: Preschoolers use exploratory approaches to selective social learning
candidates.abstract: Preschoolers evaluate many cues when making inferences about others (Harris et al., 2018). It is unclear whether children's understanding of inference-making is sophisticated enough that they alsoseek outthe most relevant cues for making specific inferences. Here, we tasked 4- and 5-year-olds and adults with a modified epistemic trust paradigm in which they were told to select one of two informants to help them learn about novel objects. However, before doing so, participants were told that they could learn up to three pieces of information about the informants: what they know (epistemic cue), how they play with their friends (benevolence cue), or what they look like (appearance cue). Of particular interest was which cue participants prioritized (picked first) and what strategies they used for seeking information. In Study 1, adults prioritized learning epistemic information and tended to employ efficient information-seeking strategies (selecting the fewest cues possible to make their inferences). Children, on the other hand, chose each cue first at relatively equal rates and tended to employ exploratory strategies for information-seeking (sampling broadly from the available information). This was even the case in Study 2, in which the informativeness of the appearance and benevolence cues was reduced. These studies raise questions about the way in which children make inferences about others and point to a tendency for children to employ exploratory strategies for learning about others (Gopnik, 2020).

candidates.title: Payoff selectivity drives collective intelligence during dynamic resource tracking in humans
candidates.abstract: Humans' abilities for complex social learning and collective adaptation stand out across species. Yet it is largely unknown how people integrate dynamically changing personal and social cues in realistic environments, resulting in collective intelligence or maladaptive behavior. Here, we report an online 3D immersive-reality experiment in which participants (n = 621) search for and track a mobile resource under realistic visual-spatial constraints. Participants complete the task either alone or in groups of five with different types of social information and resource speeds. Contrasting earlier work, participants in groups outperform solitary individuals, but only when payoff information was available. High-resolution visual field data and movement trajectories reveal that payoff visibility prompts adaptive recalibration of visual information flow, thereby enabling flexible adaptation. Computational models of fine-grained movement decisions and agent-based simulations show that payoff information lets participants dynamically identify and selectively respond to reliable social cues, thus unlocking the group's collective potential.

candidates.title: Cooperative care as a candidate mechanism linking prolonged childhood and brain expansion in human evolution
candidates.abstract: Two traits distinguish modern humans from all other primates: an exceptionally large brain and an exceptionally prolonged childhood. What mechanism produced this combination, and why are the two traits dissociated in other hominins? Standard models predict that brain size and developmental duration should co-vary tightly, yet the fossil record reveals that they do not: small-brained hominins at Dikika, Dmanisi, and Rising Star show slow development, while large-brained Neanderthals matured fast. Evolutionary simulations show that cooperative care can offer a coherent account of these dissociations. In Experiment 1, cooperative care extends childhood and, as an emergent consequence, enhances social learning independent of brain size (+32.5% childhood extension with no change in brain size), creating a knowledge–storage mismatch that generates selection pressure for brain expansion. In Experiment 2, when the metabolic ceiling is lifted through allomaternal provisioning, cooperative care populations show significant brain expansion (+34%) co-occurring with further childhood extension and enhanced social learning. In Experiment 3, when populations lacking cooperative care achieve equivalent brain expansion through dietary improvement alone, they instead mature faster, producing brain expansion decoupled from developmental prolongation. The simulation thereby identifies two emergent routes to large brains: a cooperative-care route producing coupled brain–childhood expansion, and a nutrition-only route producing brain expansion without developmental prolongation—a dissociation that parallels the comparison between modern humans and Neanderthals. These results suggest that the distinctly human developmental package may reflect not brain expansion per se, but the cooperative care system within which that expansion occurred.

candidates.title: Second-Order Visual Attention Prediction in Multiagent Videos via Emotion-Aware Belief Inference.
candidates.abstract: In human social cognition, understanding others' attention relies not only on explicit cues such as gaze and posture but also on observers' inferences of implicit factors, including emotions, task goals, and social roles. This belief-based ability, known as second-order attention modeling, is a key component of theory of mind (ToM), enabling individuals to infer others' attentional states during multiagent interactions. Existing vision systems mainly focus on first-order attention modeling, such as gaze estimation and gaze following, which predict physical gaze locations. Although effective at the perceptual level, these methods cannot capture belief formation or account for modulatory factors such as emotions, limiting their applicability to higher-level social cognition. To address this limitation, we propose a belief-driven framework for second-order attention modeling, formulating observer inference under uncertainty as conditional probability estimation and integrating emotional cues, task semantics, and social roles. The framework extends attention modeling from gaze perception to emotion-modulated belief reasoning, enabling prediction of observer-reported attentional beliefs from visual, visually inferred affective, and social-context cues when direct gaze evidence is limited or ambiguous. We further introduce a large-scale dataset with diverse agents, tasks, and emotional contexts, whose observer-reported labels are validated through test-retest analysis, together with an emotion-conditioned evaluation metric for social-cognitive assessment. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods and produces predictions consistent with observer reports, showing effectiveness for emotion-aware second-order attention modeling.

candidates.title: Patient and Family Perspectives on Statutory Duty of Candour Following Serious Adverse Patient Safety Events
candidates.abstract: BackgroundThe Statutory Duty of Candour (SDC) legally requires healthcare organisations to notify patients, families, and carers who experience a serious adverse patient safety event (SAPSE), provide an apology, and explain steps taken to prevent recurrence. However, despite growing international adoption of SDC, evidence on its implementation and impact on patients and families ('consumers') remains limited. This study examined consumer awareness, understanding, and lived experiences of SDC in Victoria, Australia, two years after its introduction.MethodsA mixed-methods study integrated data from an online survey and semi-structured interviews with healthcare consumers in Victoria, Australia. Descriptive analysis was undertaken for quantitative items, while reflexive thematic analysis was applied to qualitative data from survey free-text responses and interview transcripts.ResultsIn total, 80 consumers participated: 72 completed the survey and 13 completed interviews, with five participating in both. Although nearly two-thirds (61%) had no prior knowledge of SDC, over three-quarters (78%) perceived it as useful. Among those who had experienced an adverse event, half reported that staff were not open following the incident, over half reported that no post-incident meeting occurred, and satisfaction with meetings was low (26%). Six themes were identified: (1) Candour as Moral Reassurance; (2) Persistent Scepticism and Conditional Trust; (3) Limited Awareness and Accessibility of SDC; (4) Genuine Apology for Trust Repair; (5) Emotional Labour, Power, and the Risk of Re-traumatisation; and (6) Demonstrating Accountability with Organisational Learning and Improvement. An overarching theme, Candour as a Relational Process for Trust, described how trust was tested, repaired, or further eroded through SDC processes following an adverse event.ConclusionSDC holds significant potential to repair trust following adverse events, but its impact depends on how it is enacted. When delivered with empathy and meaningful follow-up, SDC supports repair of trust. However, when experienced as procedural or defensive, SDC may compound distress and further erode trust. Therefore, SDC must be embedded not just as a regulatory requirement, but as a relational and person-centred practice for patients and families.Patient or public contributionHealthcare consumer representatives were part of the research team, assisting with the study design, data analysis, and article writing.

candidates.title: True Co-Design: Buzzword or Breakthrough? The Value of Authentic Relationships in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Promotion
candidates.abstract: As Aboriginal women, Registered Nurses, and health promotion and public health academics, our perspectives are shaped by both our lived experiences and our professional practice. We have worked across clinical care, health promotion, public health, research, and academia, partnering with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, health services, and organisations to improve health and wellbeing. These experiences have reinforced our understanding that meaningful and sustainable health promotion is built on relationships, trust, and shared decision-making, rather than simply the application of participatory methods. We wrote this commentary because we have become increasingly concerned that the term co-design is being used widely across research, policy and practice without always reflecting the principles it was intended to represent. Too often, co-design is reduced to consultation, workshops or the collection of community feedback, while decision-making power, and control remain with researchers, institutions or health services. In our experience, this not only undermines the intent of co-design but also risks reinforcing the very inequities that health promotion seeks to address. Our understanding of authentic co-design is informed by Aboriginal ways of knowing, being and doing, which recognise that relationships are not peripheral to the work; they are the work. Genuine partnership requires time to build trust, reciprocal relationships, mutual accountability, respect for community knowledge, and a willingness to share power throughout every stage of a project. These principles are not unique to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander contexts; rather, we believe they represent the foundations of effective health promotion with all communities. As nurses and health promoters, we have seen firsthand that programs developed with communities are more relevant, culturally safe, acceptable and sustainable than those developed for communities. Conversely, we have also witnessed the consequences of tokenistic engagement, where communities are invited to participate after key decisions have already been made. These experiences have shaped our conviction that authentic co-design is not a methodology to be applied, but a way of working that is grounded in humility, reciprocity and respect. We acknowledge that our perspectives are informed by our identities as Aboriginal women and by our professional experiences. While we do not claim to speak for all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples or communities, we offer this commentary from a position of shared experience and commitment to strengthening health promotion practice. We hope this paper contributes to an ongoing conversation about moving beyond co-design as a buzzword and toward approaches that genuinely redistribute power, privilege community expertise and foster authentic relationships capable of creating meaningful and lasting health change.

candidates.title: Reciprocity in research: Participant views on return of results in the WATCH-PD qualitative study
candidates.abstract: BackgroundResearch participants increasingly desire access to their personalized results. A growing emphasis on patient engagement and recognition of participants as partners in research has intensified ethical considerations around data sharing and return of results. While some research teams have started returning personalized results, important questions remain about how to do so responsibly and effectively.ObjectiveTo explore the perspectives of people with Parkinson's on return of individual research results, including preferences regarding digital data.MethodsThis qualitative sub-study was conducted as part the WATCH-PD study (Wearable Assessments in The Clinic and at Home in PD). Online qualitative interviews to explore perceptions on return of research results were conducted annually each year from 2022-2025. Content analysis techniques were used to analyze transcripts.Results33 participants completed interviews and were included in the analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Most participants desire to receive personal results provided the results are understandable to them; (2) Knowing personal results could support disease management and future planning; and (3) Access to data is an ethical obligation of the research team and a reciprocal return of personal information.ConclusionsParticipants in this study wanted the choice to receive personal research results, and most preferred disclosure even when findings might be unfavorable. Although returning person-level data presents logistical and ethical challenges, engaging participants as partners through transparent data sharing may strengthen engagement, trust, and advance patient-centered research.

candidates.title: Inclusion That Excludes: Rethinking the Ecological Model for Mental Disability Through Defensive Dynamics, Institutional Power, and Capital Asymmetries
candidates.abstract: This article offers a critical reworking of ecological and social-ecological models as applied to intellectual and developmental disabilities, autism, and severe mental illness. Drawing on a qualitative synthesis of 18 studies, we show that ecological frameworks are predominantly used as descriptive mapping devices, that power and inequalities enter analyses in partial and fragmented ways, and that intersystemic connections often generate formally inclusive yet experientially exclusionary arrangements. To address these limitations, we propose an Integrated Ecological Model for Mental Disability, which retains Bronfenbrenner's multilevel architecture but introduces four structural extensions: asymmetry of reciprocity in the microsystem, the defensive mesosystem, capital-modulated exosystemic permeability, and the performative and normalizing exosystem. These concepts integrate Bourdieu's theory of capital and field, Foucault's genealogy of dispositifs,1 and group psychoanalysis, and they are grounded in recurrent patterns observed across school transitions, family-service relations, residential services, and autism employment programs. The framework has implications for research designs that move beyond barriers and facilitators for multilevel clinical and educational interventions, and for normative debates on relational justice and psychopolitical validity in mental-disability policy.

candidates.title: Same-sex attention and cooperation biases following digital social exclusion: Female users' responses to gender-coded virtual agents
candidates.abstract: As digital interactions proliferate, social exclusion in online collaboration has become a notable social experience. This study investigates whether different digital collaborative contexts are associated with female users' early processing of gaze cues and resource allocation toward gender-coded virtual agents. Utilizing a 3 (Exclusion Context: male-group exclusion, female-group exclusion, mixed-gender inclusion) × 2 (Agent Gender: female-coded, male-coded) × 2 (SOA: 200 ms, 800 ms) mixed design, this research included 200 female participants and integrated an online collaborative task, a gaze-cueing task, and a one-shot Trust Game. Results indicated that, compared to the mixed-gender inclusion context, participants in the male-group exclusion context exhibited a greater gaze-cueing effect toward female-coded agents at the 200 ms SOA and allocated more tokens to them. In the female-group exclusion context, an equivalent prioritized allocation to female-coded agents did not emerge, and participants retained more tokens. An exploratory analysis focusing on the male-group exclusion and inclusion contexts further revealed a statistical indirect association between the early gaze-cueing effect and subsequent investment; however, this result cannot establish a causal mediating mechanism. Overall, this study provides preliminary evidence that digital exclusion contexts are associated with attentional and cooperative biases toward same-sex-coded agents. Given that the three contexts simultaneously altered exclusion status, team gender, and team composition, and that the sample comprised solely female participants from a single region, the conclusions should be restricted to contextual behavioral differences and cannot be viewed as direct evidence of a "female alliance" or gender-specific mechanisms.

candidates.title: Learning to take up space: A mindfulness reflection
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe attitudes of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, nonjudging, patience, trust, beginner's mind, nonstriving, and letting go, offer valuable guidance for today's strained health care environments. These principles gradually informed the development of a Nurse Practitioner (NP) and Physician Associate (PA) Fellowship program designed to support NPs and PAs transitioning into complex specialty neurology practice. Mindfulness became the fellowship's implicit foundation, encouraging psychological safety, reciprocity, and belonging. This reflection examines how mindfulness informed the fellowship's culture and the development of sustainable professional identities.

candidates.title: Longitudinal Measurement Invariance of the Autism Impact Measure (AIM) in Children and Adolescents With Autism
candidates.abstract: PurposeThe Autism Impact Measure (AIM) is a caregiver-reported measure that assesses behavioral changes in response to treatment in children with autism. This study evaluated its longitudinal measurement invariance, which is critical for ensuring that observed score changes reflect true behavioral change rather than construct-irrelevant variance.MethodsThe sample comprised a large clinical cohort from the Autism Treatment Network (ATN) Registry (N = 597; baseline Mage = 9.7 years, SD = 3.3). Using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis and established fit criteria, we examined the longitudinal measurement invariance of the AIM scores among participants with longitudinal data (n = 371) approximately 1 year later (M = 1.17 years; SD = 0.28).ResultsThe AIM scores demonstrated longitudinal configural, metric, and scalar measurement invariance within participants across the one-year interval for all symptom domains: Repetitive Behavior, Communication, Atypical Behavior, Social Reciprocity, and Peer Interaction.ConclusionThese findings provide validity evidence for the interpretation that observed changes in AIM scores across time reflect genuine differences in autism symptom presentation rather than shifts in item functioning, thereby further supporting the AIM's use as a longitudinal symptom tracking tool in autism treatment.

candidates.title: Relational Capital as a Welfare Input: Trust, Underinvestment, and Institution-Sensitive Correction
candidates.abstract: Abstract    Economic analysis routinely models physical, human, and institutional capital, yet the relational conditions that make cooperation valuable are often treated as background.
