This article develops a formal welfare model in which relational investment generates an individually enjoyed good and a spillover that improves the relational experience of others. Trust is represented as a productivity parameter that determines how effectively one person’s investment enters another person’s relational payoff. The model yields four main results. First, a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium exists under standard convex-cost conditions. Second, decentralized relational investment is inefficiently low whenever relational spillovers are positive. Third, greater trust has a paradoxical comparative-static effect: it reduces private relational effort through free riding while increasing socially optimal effort, so the underinvestment wedge widens as the relational technology improves. Fourth, a state-contingent corrective subsidy can decentralize the social optimum, but its desirability is weakened when monetary intervention crowds out intrinsic relational valuation. An institutional extension endogenizes trust through investments in settings that support repeated, respectful interaction. Numerical illustrations map the analytic results and show how corrective policy becomes more important as relational spillovers increase. The framework connects civil-economy accounts of reciprocity and relational goods with conventional externality theory while preserving the distinctive feature that relationships are jointly produced and partly noncontractible. It provides a tractable basis for analyzing welfare, institutional design, and policy when human flourishing depends on the quality of social interaction as well as material consumption.  JEL classification:  A13; D62; D63; D91; Z13

candidates.title: Temporal dynamics of grooming reciprocity in crested macaques: do social bonds affect exchange?
candidates.abstract: Primates maintain cooperative relationships largely through grooming reciprocity, yet studies disagree on the timescales over which grooming is returned. Part of this disagreement stems from statistical issues: inconsistent definitions of a reciprocation window, combined with the exclusion of unreciprocated grooming, leave the debate unresolved. We still do not know if primates exchange grooming within the short windows predicted by biological market theory or over much longer timescales. Whilst survival analysis can identify reciprocation windows objectively by retaining unreciprocated grooming as censored data, previous studies have applied it inconsistently. This inconsistency leaves the true time frames over which primates reciprocate grooming somewhat blurred. Here, we use a statistical approach that addresses these problems to examine grooming reciprocity in crested macaques (  Macaca nigra ), a socially tolerant macaque species. We applied survival analysis to identify each group’s short-term reciprocation window without imposing arbitrary cut-offs, and Bayesian survival models to test whether social bond strength and eigenvector centrality predicted reciprocation latency. Short-term reciprocation occurred rarely (29% of events in one group and 5% in the other); most reciprocation occurred over longer timescales than previous research commonly assumes. Stronger bonds predicted faster reciprocation; this finding suggests that crested macaques express social investment in valued partners through how promptly they return grooming, meaning that the timing of exchange carries information about relationship value. Eigenvector centrality showed no credible effect, though our small sample size and dense groups prevent us from interpreting this outcome more robustly. Substantial variation between dyads remained unexplained, pointing to partner-specific properties we have yet to identify. These findings caution against assuming that reciprocity operates over short windows. They show that social predictors, such as bond strength, remain essential to understanding when primates return grooming. This work provides a baseline for testing whether grooming is exchanged for other social commodities, and for comparing reciprocation timescales across macaque species that differ in social tolerance.

candidates.title: The Influence of Considering Others' Emotions on Children's Resource Distribution
candidates.abstract: Understanding how one's actions affect others' emotions is an important aspect of prosocial development. Extending prior findings with adults, this study investigated whether predicting future emotional messages from the recipient could enhance preschoolers' altruistic sharing. In Experiment 1, 4- to 6-year-old Korean children played a dictator game in which they allocated stickers between themselves and a monkey puppet. The children in the experimental condition were informed that the monkey would draw a picture of how he felt about the number of stickers received, while those in the control condition received no such information. Children in the experimental condition shared more generously overall, particularly among 4- and 5-year-olds. Six-year-olds allocated resources about equally between two conditions, resembling Korean adults' preference for equality observed in a pilot study. Experiment 2 tested whether the effect was driven specifically by considering others' emotions rather than anticipating feedback in general. Children were told they would receive an unspecified 'message' from the recipient, but no differences in sharing emerged between conditions. Thus, just anticipating any message or feedback from the recipient did not promote children's altruistic resource allocation. The results suggest that considering others' emotions promotes altruistic behaviours in young children.

candidates.title: Impact analysis of institutional framework and policy preferences with Bayesian structural equation
candidates.abstract: Mediation analysis is able to deeply analyze the finer mechanism of the path of exposure variables leading to outcome variables and has received extensive attention in many fields in recent years. In order to further analyze China's energy cooperation with neighboring countries, this paper divides the two stages of policy formulation and implementation. It connects the logical chain of "cooperation policy preferences at the decision-making level, final cooperation policy preferences to energy trade and investment cooperation." By constructing a partial Bayesian structural equation model, we verify the mediating effect played by final cooperative policy preferences. The mediation analysis based on structural equation modeling provides the possibility to analyze the complex structure among variables, including the mediation effect. And Bayesian SEM can provide a more flexible program for the construction and estimation of complex models. In addition, this paper explores the statistical analysis strategy of mediation analysis of Bayesian structural equation modeling and its statistical performance under different data characteristics through example analysis. The empirical results show that policy preferences play a significant mediating role between institutional frameworks and energy cooperation outcomes. Specifically, the Bayesian SEM estimates a positive indirect effect of 0.305, with a standard error of 0.123, a 95% confidence interval of (0.061, 0.552), and a significance level of p = 0.006. This indicates that institutional arrangements promote energy cooperation mainly by shaping policy preferences rather than through direct effects alone. Compared with classical regression-based mediation, classical SEM, Bayesian regression, and other alternative approaches, Bayesian SEM demonstrates stronger performance in handling latent-variable uncertainty, interval estimation, and parameter stability. Across the 12 estimation methods employed in this study, the estimated indirect effects range from 0.271 to 0.312 and remain consistently significant, confirming the robustness of the mediation mechanism. This indicates that while maintaining directional consistency, it offers more robust and reliable handling of latent variables and uncertainty.

candidates.title: How negative parenting relates to adolescents’ perceptions of older adults: the roles of empathy and intergenerational contact
candidates.abstract: Introduction Grounded in social learning theory, this study examines how negative parenting practices are associated with adolescents’ perceptions of older adults and investigates the roles of empathy and intergenerational contact in this process. Methods Data were collected from 2,011 Chinese adolescents using a three-wave longitudinal design. Structural equation modeling was used to test the hypothesized relationships. Results Negative parenting was significantly associated with less favorable evaluations of older adults on both the warmth and competence dimensions. Empathy mediated these relationships. Intergenerational contact further moderated the association between empathy and adolescents’ perceptions of older adults. Specifically, the indirect effects of negative parenting through empathy varied according to adolescents’ levels of intergenerational contact. Discussion These findings highlight family socialization as an important developmental context for adolescents’ perceptions of older adults and identify empathy as a key socio-emotional mechanism linking parenting experiences to intergenerational cognition.

candidates.title: It is time to revisit the external determinants of state terror
candidates.abstract: Authoritarian regimes are frequently influenced by external policies and transnational relationships when shaping domestic repression strategies. Existing empirical research has largely focused on demonstration and diffusion effects, emphasizing how governments emulate repressive practices observed abroad. Similarly, recent scholarship on authoritarian cooperation and regional organizations has argued that interstate cooperation strengthens authoritarian rule and facilitates repression through exchanges of information, expertise, resources, and strategic support. We distinguished theoretically between observational diffusion and cooperative interaction and examine empirically how each shapes state terror. Using spatial autoregressive combined models and global data on authoritarian regimes from 1947 to 2010, we found that demonstration via observational diffusion among institutionally similar regimes is generally associated with higher levels of state terror, whereas contemporaneous interdependence among such regimes is associated with lower levels. These results are broadly consistent across different specifications of the dependent variable. Our findings suggest a more nuanced relationship between interstate cooperation and repression: Cooperation may enhance authoritarian control while reducing reliance on the most extreme forms of violence. More broadly, the results indicate that diffusion-centered approaches may conflate observational learning with broader forms of authoritarian interdependence, thereby mischaracterizing the consequences of external influence for state terror.

candidates.title: Developing Gender Effective Coaches: Addressing the Knowledge to Application Gap
candidates.abstract: In recent years, there has been an increase in opportunities for women and girls in sport in Canada. Yet, biases, stereotypes, and norms about gender remain deeply embedded within sport culture (Goorevich & LaVoi, 2025), affecting girls and women across the landscape. The purpose of this doctoral dissertation was to provide coaches with evidence-based tools for their pursuit of gaining confidence in addressing and deconstructing gender beliefs that affect their coaching practice through three interconnected studies. The studies included: (1) the narrative exploration of gender beliefs and the impact they have on coaching methodologies, athlete interactions, and self-confidence; (2) the creation of a gender-related coaching self-efficacy scale; and (3) the exploration of coaches' knowledge-to-action processes through the lens of social learning. In this pursuit, I aimed to support coaches in their development of gender responsive and transformative practices to better address the needs of girls in sport. A pragmatic philosophical orientation, informed epistemologically by social constructionism, was used in this dissertation research. In line with pragmatism, a mixed methods design approach was executed taking into consideration four theoretical frameworks including a combined model of coach self-efficacy (Feltz et al., 1999) and coach effectiveness (Horn, 2002; 2008; Côté & Gilbert, 2009), Wenger's (1998) theory of social learning and communities of practice, and Goorevich and LaVoi's (2025) continuum of gendered sport coach discourses. The results of this inquiry are presented through three articles. In the first study, entirely qualitative in nature, I present composite vignettes that explored the diverse and context-dependent experiences of coaches coaching girls, further nuanced by the lived realities of women coaches. Data collection consisted of focus groups with 20 coaches ranging in sport and coaching experience. This narrative inquiry aims to illustrate how coaching philosophies and practices are socially shaped through gendered discourses operating within sport. As a result of the findings from this examination, potential items for the scale development study were created. The need for more opportunities for coaches to develop self-awareness regarding their gender biases, reflect, and deconstruct their gender beliefs to make changes to their coaching practices was also highlighted as future areas for growth in coach education. The second study was conducted through a mixed methods approach, consisting of the development and primary validation of the Girls-Centred Coaching Self-Efficacy Scale (GCSES). The scale development process followed previously established methodological guidelines (i.e., Boateng et al., 2018) with an initial 87 items being created through theory-driven item construction, coach focus groups (n = 20), expert review (n = 6), and cognitive interviews with coaches (n = 4). The revised instrument after this process included 31 items and was administered to 216 sport coaches. An exploratory factor analysis supported a four-factor structure for 23 final items accounting for 54.9% of the variance with strong internal consistency across subscales (⍺ = .80-.92). Subscales include: (1) gender literacy in coaching, (2) understanding gendered sport experiences, (3) fostering gender-inclusive sport, and (4) girl-centred coaching practices. The findings from this study provide evidence for the GCSES to be used as a context-specific tool for evaluations and interventions aimed at advancing gender responsive and transformative coaching practices. The third study used a mixed methods quasi-experimental design, exploring coaches' knowledge-to-action processes related to their girl-centred coaching self-efficacy through a combined online and social learning intervention. Twenty-five coaches took part in one of two conditions over a five-month period, either completing the series of Coaching HER's foundational eLearning modules by themselves or engaging in a community of practice (CoP; Wenger, 1998) concurrent with the eLearning modules. Coaches in both groups took the GCSES pre- and post-intervention, and data were analyzed using mixed ANOVAs. Participants in the CoP condition were also invited to partake in a focus group (n = 6) grounded in the value creation framework (VCF; Wenger-Trayner & Wenger-Trayner, 2020) to explore how value was created through their participation in the CoP. Effect and contribution data were collected throughout the intervention period (Wenger-Trayner et al., 2019). Although the study was underpowered to detect statistically significant differences between conditions, coaches who engaged in the CoP condition demonstrated small trends of mean improvements across all GCSES factors compared to the eLearning condition. Qualitative data, presented through two value creation stories (VCSs; Wenger-Trayner et al., 2019) and individual value cycle examples, aided in providing insight into the GCSES results as well as how coaches in the CoP condition translated learnings into changes to their practices. Altogether, the findings from the final study in this dissertation suggested that engagement in a CoP fostered opportunities for self-reflection, accountability, and contextual application of knowledge. Recommendations included the continued use of social learning in tandem with eLearning for coaching education to better support coaches' knowledge-to-action processes and the value of mixed methods research in this domain. The results of this doctoral dissertation aim to provide an evidence-based foundation for understanding, measuring, and supporting coaches' development toward more girl-centred and gender-equitable coaching practices. Collectively, the findings advance both theory and practice by offering practical tools, empirical evidence, and a conceptual framework to guide future coach education, research, and organizational efforts aimed at fostering meaningful and sustainable gender equity in sport.

candidates.title: The Internalization of Inclusive and Adaptive Values in Bullying Prevention Among Students at Girls’ Islamic Boarding School
candidates.abstract: Bullying remains a concern in Islamic boarding schools (pesantren), where intensive residential interactions may create complex social dynamics among students. This study aims to identify the inclusive and adaptive values developed at Al-Ishlahiyyah Girls’ Islamic Boarding School, Wonorejo, East Java, Indonesia, examine how these values are internalized through everyday educational and social practices, and analyze their contribution to bullying prevention. A qualitative approach with an intrinsic case study design was employed. Data were collected through participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and document analysis involving the boarding school caregiver, ustadzah, dormitory supervisors, senior students, and junior students. Data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification, supported by source triangulation, method triangulation, and an audit trail. The findings identified four interrelated values: tolerance, empathy, equality, and social justice. These values were internalized through four interconnected mechanisms: modeling, habituation, mentoring, and institutional policy structures. The findings further indicate that these mechanisms were associated with more inclusive verbal interactions, reduced relational exclusion, greater psychological and emotional security, and a reorientation of senior–junior relations from domination toward guidance and support. Drawing on social learning theory, the study demonstrates that bullying prevention may be understood as a socio-cultural process in which values are learned, reinforced, and enacted through everyday interactions and institutional practices. The study contributes a context-sensitive perspective on value internalization as a preventive dimension of bullying in girls’ Islamic boarding schools

candidates.title: Selective Epistemic Trust and the Recovery of Agency After Interpersonal Trauma
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Interpersonal trauma can disturb how people evaluate communicated information, yet greater willingness to accept advice is an ambiguous marker of psychological recovery. A person may become more receptive to useful guidance while also becoming less able to question unreliable authority. This critical integrative review examines whether selective epistemic trust offers a more defensible clinical objective than increasing trust alone. Targeted searches of biomedical records, publisher resources, and relevant reference lists informed a synthesis of developmental theory, psychometric research, psychotherapy process studies, and scholarship on epistemic injustice. The evidence supports distinguishing trust, mistrust, and credulity, but associations with symptoms vary across instruments and populations. Recent behavioural and observational studies extend assessment beyond self-report, although they do not establish that increasing advice acceptance causes recovery after trauma. The article develops an evaluative framework connecting sensitivity to information quality with the patient's capacity to question, revise, and retain ownership of decisions. Its central proposition is that therapeutic benefit should include learning from credible communication without making agreement with the clinician the criterion of improvement. A proposed research programme separates source reliability, emotional safety, prior confidence, and the consequences of error; combines repeated behavioural assessment with session observation and patient-defined outcomes; and tests whether changes generalise beyond the treatment relationship. Competing explanations include symptom relief, alliance quality, task familiarity, and accommodation to authority. Selective trust remains a candidate process requiring prospective validation. Its immediate contribution is to clarify what successful social learning should preserve: openness to evidence together with meaningful authorship of personal choices.

candidates.title: Documentation of co-creation and data supporting the development of a serious game for social skills
candidates.abstract: Abstract Adolescence is a critical period for the maturation of brain regions underlying social cognition, such as socio-moral reasoning (SMR) and decision-making. Adolescents—and adults who work with them—should have access to validated pedagogical tools and effective resources to support their social learning during this period. These tools are especially important when social or affective deficits are identified, given these can lead to maladaptive behaviors or mental health problems. However, few learning or intervention tools aimed at improving socio-moral reasoning and decision-making exist. The design of such tools should consider factors related to validity and youth engagement to ensure uptake and thus requires a break from traditional approaches. In response to this challenge, the Are you GAME? project aims to develop a serious video game (i.e., an interactive digital game designed for purposes beyond entertainment) designed to target socio-moral reasoning and decision-making abilities in adolescents. We present findings from four recherche-creation phases (Gamestorm session, Focus groups with adolescents, Focus groups with educators, Playtests) involving diverse co-creation partners (researchers, industry partners, user groups) to ensure transparency, support reproducibility, and inform future work in serious game design. The research-creation process comprised 15 co-creation sessions involving 72 participants, including adolescents, educators, researchers, and game design professionals. Qualitative data consisting of field notes, audio recordings, and written reports were analyzed through documentation across successive research-creation cycles. Preliminary Playtest results indicate that the game is a promising tool for promoting youth social competence.

candidates.title: Physiological synchrony predicts reduced reciprocity only in face-to-face interactions
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
candidates.abstract: Across species, cooperative decisions are often asymmetric: one individual risks their own resources before knowing whether others will reciprocate. Such uncertainty is central to the evolution of trust and reciprocal exchanges. Physiological synchrony is frequently assumed to support cooperation, yet it remains unclear both how synchrony arises and how it functions in these asymmetric social interactions. We tested whether mutual visibility shapes physiological synchrony, and whether synchrony in turn predicts cooperative behaviour in repeated trust-reciprocity exchanges. Skin conductance synchrony was stronger and more temporally aligned when individuals interacted face-to-face, yet facial expressivity did not account for this effect. Contrary to the dominant perspective, higher synchrony predicted reduced reciprocity, and only when partners could see each other. Exploratory analyses suggested that this negative link depended on arousal, indicating that the social function of synchrony is shaped by both mutual visibility and the affective state of the individual involved. These findings show that physiological synchrony is not a uniformly prosocial mechanism but a context-dependent phenomenon that can undermine cooperation under certain conditions, offering insight into the mechanisms and the function of synchrony in shaping cooperative exchanges.

candidates.title: Foundational Principles of Effective E-Mentoring
candidates.abstract: Abstract Effective e-mentoring requires intentional design grounded in relational principles that transcend technological tools. This chapter establishes four foundational principles: trust as the bedrock of mentoring relationships, reciprocity that honors mutual growth and learning, boundaries that protect both mentors and mentees from overextension while maintaining authentic connection, and developmental orientation that centers long-term growth over transactional problem-solving. These principles operate differently in digital environments where relational cues are limited and interactions feel more formal. The chapter explores how trust must be actively built through consistency and transparency, how reciprocity manifests in digital contexts, how boundaries require explicit negotiation around response times and availability, and how developmental mentoring resists quick-fix solutions in favor of sustained support. Rather than providing prescriptive templates, the chapter offers practitioners a conceptual framework for designing e-mentoring that remains human-centered, relationally grounded, and developmentally sound regardless of platform or modality.

candidates.title: Navigating rénqíng and face: A four-phase sequential model of money-borrowing requests in rural China
candidates.abstract: Abstract In rural China, money-borrowing is not merely a financial transaction but a complex social practice. This study explores the pragmatic strategies of money-borrowing requests through qualitative interviews with 29 rural residents. The analysis identifies a four-phase sequential model that maps the communicative architecture of these requests, comprising (1) a preparatory and framing phase; (2) a core request phase; (3) a support phase involving facework, justification, and reciprocity; and (4) a potential intensification and coercion phase. Furthermore, the analysis shows how recurrent strategy patterns reveal the cultural script for negotiating trust, face, and rénqíng (人情). Four core components of this script are identified: the primacy of relational framing through fictive kinship; the function of justification and hearer consideration as prerequisites; the verbal construction of trust through promises; and a structural preference for indirectness as a risk management strategy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that money-borrowing in rural China is not a simple economic transaction but a socially embedded practice, systematically shaped by the cultural logic of rénqíng and face. More broadly, the study argues that high-stakes requests should be analyzed not merely as inventories of individual strategies, but as sequentially organized, culturally saturated communicative events through which social obligations, interpersonal trust, and face dynamics are pragmatically constituted.

candidates.title: Developmental sensitivities and strengths in adolescent mentors of community children: A phenomenological study with youth in U.S. urban communities of color stressed by low-income
candidates.venue: Journal of Human Behavior in the Social Environment
candidates.abstract: Cross-age mentoring programs provide adolescents with opportunities to develop leadership, empathy, and self-efficacy while supporting younger peers. However, little is known about the developmental sensitivities and strengths adolescent mentors bring to cross-age mentoring relationships, particularly among youth of color in economically stressed communities. Guided by a phenomenological and ecological systems framework, this study examined how adolescent mentors self-evaluated their mentoring competence and interpreted their mentees’ responsiveness at the beginning of their cross-age mentoring program. Data were drawn from 316 debriefing forms completed by 158 mentors participating in the Saving Lives Inspiring Youth (SLIY) program in urban communities of color in a largeMidwestern city. Qualitative thematic and content analyses identified 17 categories of responses reflecting mentors’ cognitive schemas regarding confidence and caring. Most mentors attributed their confidence to their mentees’ openness and engagement, highlighting how perceived relational reciprocity fostered their self-efficacy and fulfillment. Mentors also emphasized their strengths as shared experiences of hardship, their empathy, and being community role models. Findings reveal that adolescent mentors’ self-efficacy is deeply relational and context-dependent, shaped by their developmental stage, social sensitivity, and cultural wealth. These results expand understanding of mentoring as a developmental and community-embedded process, affirming the value of adolescents’ lived experiences and resilience in fostering meaningful intergenerational connections. Programs that support adolescent mentors through reflective supervision, enhance their empathy, and include culturally responsive instructions may improve match quality and promote sustained mentor–mentee engagement.

candidates.title: FLEX AND RADICALLY OPEN DBT: Points of Continuity, Divergence, and Neuro-Affirming Adaptation
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Radically Open Dialectical Behavior Therapy (RO-DBT) provides an establishedtransdiagnostic framework for understanding and treating maladaptive overcontrol. Itsemphasis on radical openness, self-inquiry, social signaling, social safety, behavioralexperimentation, and interpersonal connectedness provides an important conceptualfoundation for FLEX. FLEX retains many of these principles while modifying their clinicalinterpretation through a more explicitly neuro-affirming, contextual, and relational lens.This comparative white paper examines areas of continuity and divergence between FLEXand traditional RO-DBT, with particular attention to the treatment of neurodivergent clients.The central distinction is not whether social signaling and openness matter, but how atypicalsignaling is interpreted and what constitutes meaningful therapeutic change. FLEX cautionsagainst assuming that reduced eye contact, limited facial affect, atypical prosody,preference for solitude, need for predictability, masking, or reduced social responsivenessnecessarily represent pathological overcontrol. Instead, these behaviors are evaluated according to function, nervous-system state, individual neurobiology, environmentaldemands, personal values, and relational context. FLEX further distinguishes deliberate or protective masking from nervous-system depletionand emphasizes that observable flatness, withdrawal, or reduced expressiveness mayreflect sensory overload, fatigue, processing demands, or an individual's naturalcommunication style rather than interpersonal avoidance. Accordingly, FLEX shifts someemphasis from modifying the client's social presentation toward improving mutualintelligibility within relationships. Clients may learn to communicate their internal statemore directly while trusted others learn the individual's unique patterns of signaling—aprocess described within FLEX as providing a relational “decoder ring.” Additional areas of divergence include FLEX's explicit use of self-compassion as acounterbalance to self-inquiry and accountability; its emphasis on mutual accommodationrather than unilateral social adaptation; its conceptualization of masking and unmasking ascontext-dependent choices; and its focus on selective, reciprocal, and earned vulnerability.FLEX also broadens assessment of emotional and interpersonal behavior to includesensory load, physical state, processing capacity, fatigue, pain, stress, and other contextualvariables that may affect an individual's capacity for connection. These modifications converge around a broader treatment target termed relationalflexibility: the ability to remain connected to oneself while adapting to context,communicating needs and internal experience, tolerating uncertainty and feedback, andpermitting appropriate influence from other people without abandoning autonomy,boundaries, or neurodivergent identity. FLEX therefore should not be understood as a rejection or replacement of RO-DBT. Rather,it represents an emerging clinical extension and reinterpretation of overcontrol treatmentthat places neurodivergent experience, individualized communication, contextual capacity,relational reciprocity, and mutual accommodation closer to the center of formulation. Thispaper describes conceptual distinctions between the models and identifies hypothesesrequiring future empirical investigation; it does not establish comparative efficacy betweenFLEX and RO-DBT.

candidates.title: Biases in individual and social decision-making
candidates.abstract: Human behavior is shaped by the interplay between innate response tendencies and experience–dependent learning. Automatic Pavlovian reactions, i.e. approach to potential rewards and inhibition in the face of potential punishments, often facilitate rapid, adaptive action, yet they can conflict with instrumental demands that require acting (or withholding action) contrary to these biases. This thesis investigates how such biases shape learning and decision–making and how social contexts modulate their expression. A central theme is that overcoming Pavlovian–instrumental conflict carries measurable mental effort, and that social evaluation selectively perturbs the mechanisms supporting action generation and reward processing. I take a behavioral, physiological and computational approach to (i) formalize Pavlovian–instrumental interactions in reinforcement learning, (ii) quantify the mental effort involved in decision–making under incongruency using pupillometry and (iii) dissociate the effects of mere social presence and social evaluation on learning. First, I synthesize prior theoretical and empirical work to motivate a reinforcement learning framework in which Pavlovian value signals invigorate or suppress action independently of instrumental contingencies, while frontal control processes can down–regulate these influences when they are maladaptive. Within this framework, I derive testable predictions linking latent variables (action values, prediction errors, and Pavlovian conflict) to both behavior choices, reaction times) and trial–by–trial task–evoked pupillary responses as a proxy for arousal/effort. I then test these predictions in a Go/NoGo learning paradigm that orthogonalizes action requirements (Go vs. NoGo) and outcome valence (reward vs. punishment). Across seven candidate reinforcement learning models, variants that include a Pavlovian component (reward→invigoration, punishment→inhibition) best explain human behavior, and the simplest of these, with a single outcome sensitivity and a learned Pavlovian value, wins; model and parameter recovery confirm that this conclusion is identifiable. Behaviorally, participants are more accurate under congruent mappings (rewarded actions and preventive inactions) than under incongruent ones (omission schedule and active avoidance), with the omission schedule particularly impaired, and respond faster for reward than for punishment. Physiologically, the task-evoked pupil response differentiates trial types by Pavlovian–instrumental congruence at the cue, by the executed action at the decision, and by losses and omitted rewards at the outcome. Time–resolved model–based analyses ground these effects in the latent variables of the winning model: the learned Pavlovian value scales the pupil during cue evaluation and drives dilation at the decision when it opposes the required action, while an unsigned Pavlovian prediction error, i.e. surprise irrespective of its sign, governs the outcome–locked response. At every stage the pupil tracks the Pavlovian rather than the instrumental quantity, linking latent learning signals to physiological effort. To assess social modulation, I repeat the task within subjects across three contexts: individual performance, passive social presence and active social evaluation with contingent payoffs. Social evaluation produces a selective deficit in action learning: participants show impaired acquisition and execution of Go responses while NoGo learning remains intact. Concomitantly, phasic pupillary responses associated with action requirements are attenuated under evaluation, consistent with a reduction in available cognitive resources or altered noradrenergic arousal when decisions are made under social judgment. Despite stable average Pavlovian and Go biases across contexts, evaluation shifts Positivity bias (reward vs. avoidance performance) toward negative values, indicating a conservative reweighting of reward processing in evaluative settings. Together, these findings provide a unified account of how Pavlovian biases shape human learning and choice, how cognitive control overcomes these biases at measurable physiological cost, and how social evaluation selectively disrupts action generation and reward processing. The work clarifies the computational roles of Pavlovian and instrumental systems, grounds the pupil response in model–derived variables resolved across the course of a decision, and isolates social evaluation, distinct from mere presence, as a driver of action–specific learning impairments. Limitations include the interpretive specificity of pupillometry and the need to generalize beyond the Go/NoGo domain; I outline multi–method extensions (EEG/fMRI/pharmacology) and broader decision paradigms (risk, delay, effort). Overall, the thesis advances a testable framework for understanding when and why humans fail to act optimally, even when they “know better”, and how social environments can tip the balance between reflexive and goal–directed control.

candidates.title: Theory of Scene: Breaking the Symmetry Trap in Multi-Agent LLM Coordination
candidates.abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are largely homogeneous, as their agents behave alike even across distinct LLMs. We show that when such agents act concurrently without communication, they collide on targets they must split and diverge on targets they must take together, a double failure we term the symmetry trap. Theory of Mind (ToM), widely used for coordination without communication, cannot escape this trap, since homogeneous agents form the same prediction of one another and respond to it in the same way. We propose Theory of Scene (ToS), a training-free reasoning schema in which each agent reads its public role, the only difference between the agents, and the task context they all observe. Homogeneous agents thereby derive one division of labor, each taking the part its role fixes, which turns homogeneity from the cause of the trap into the cure. ToS reads the role together with the scene through role gating, which determines whether ownership overlaps or is already divided, and the task context through task coupling, which infers whether the team must converge on each target, divide it, or take its stages in turn. We evaluate on DivvyBench, a controlled environment we introduce, whose target types make an episode Competitive, Cooperative, or Mixed across Tabletop, Airspace, and Household scenarios, and on two established agentic benchmarks, GovSim and Overcooked. ToS outperforms all six baselines on every benchmark, and each baseline falls far behind it in at least one setting. Against ToM given the same inputs, ToS raises the DivvyBench success rate from 71.1% to 99.6%, the GovSim total gain from 207 to 400, and the Overcooked level-normalized throughput from 1.41 to 1.67.

candidates.title: When and Why are Social Categories Overused Relative to Individuating Information? A Bayesian Approach to Identifying Biases in Impression Formation Processes
candidates.abstract: When making inferences about others, people often need to integrate multiple types of information, including the person’s social categories (e.g., occupation) as well as other “individuating” information (e.g., their behaviors). The current work re-examines this integration process, to understand when and why it produces biases involving over-reliance on category information. We identify two key challenges in identifying such biases, and develop a novel Bayesian modelling approach to overcome them. As a first step in applying this approach, the current work examined a set of novel predictions based on viewing the Continuum Model of impression formation in light of this Bayesian approach. Specifically, a series of six studies tested whether occupation categories might be overused in general, or especially in conditions thought to reduce effortful processing (i.e., greater cognitive load or information consistency). Results showed no evidence of category overuse, nor of shifts in this direction, in any of these conditions (though some ambiguity remained about the load manipulation’s effectiveness). This provides initial evidence against the idea that intrinsic differences in how these categories are processed or represented will lead to their overuse. A seventh study provided the first direct evidence of a case where categories were overused: when contextual factors (i.e., background goals) made them the category especially relevant, while processing resources were limited. More broadly, the current work developed the theoretical and methodological foundations for identifying category overuse that stems from biased inference processes, and demonstrated the power of this approach for understanding when and why such biases occur.

candidates.title: Dimensional and Categorical Predictors of Theory of Mind Network Activation: A transdiagnostic fMRI Study in Psychiatric Inpatients
candidates.abstract: Socio-cognitive alterations are widely observed across different psychiatric conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these deficits map onto distinct diagnostic categories or represent a shared transdiagnostic phenotype, driven by dimensional psychopathological symptom severity.This study evaluates Theory of Mind (ToM) network activation during a naturalistic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) movie paradigm in 313 participants, including 91 healthy controls and 222 psychiatric inpatients across five distinct diagnostic clusters (substance use, schizophrenia spectrum, affective, anxiety, and personality disorders). Frequentist analyses revealed decreased ToM-selective activity in psychiatric patients, compared to controls across all ToM regions of interest (ROIs). No significant difference emerged between diagnostic groups, but ROI activation correlated negatively with Adult Self-Report (ASR) scales (  Total Problems, Internalising, Externalising ). Subsequent Bayesian analysis of covariance (ANCOVAs) consistently favoured models that excluded traditional categorical diagnoses, suggesting that dimensional measures, especially Total Problems and Internalising, provided substantially greater predictive utility for ToM-related regional brain activation. Our findings challenge traditional categorical classifications in neurobiological research as they suggest that atypical mentalising might reflect a shared transdiagnostic vulnerability.  Highlights  Reduced Theory of Mind specific activation in psychiatric inpatients presents as a shared, transdiagnostic feature. Theory of Mind specific activation shows no disorder-specific patterns across five distinct clinical diagnostic clusters. Bayesian analyses consistently favour continuous psychopathology dimensions over categorical classifications in predicting Theory of Mind specific activation

candidates.title: Cerebellar anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) improves implicit mentalizing sequence learning: A double-blind sham-controlled study
candidates.abstract: An increasing number of studies have revealed that the posterior cerebellum plays a vital role in mentalizing by identifying and learning social action sequences that render social interaction more fluent, coordinated, and predictable. An implicit social sequencing task, the Belief serial response time (SRT) task, was administered during and 30 min after targeting the cerebellum with anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; 2 mA for 20 min, electrode 2 cm below the inion). In a previous study, this setup did not show significant improvement in response times. We reasoned that the familiar and overlearned nature of attributing social beliefs resulted in a ceiling effect and thus left very little margin for improvement on the task. The current study developed a more difficult version of the Belief SRT task. Using a double-blind sham-controlled protocol, 60 participants received either anodal tDCS or sham tDCS using the same stimulation protocol. Results showed that participants receiving anodal tDCS responded faster when the sequence of actions was repeated as opposed to totally randomized compared with participants who received sham tDCS. These findings suggest a positive effect of anodal cerebellar tDCS on implicit mentalizing sequence learning, supporting a causal role of the cerebellum in this learning process. This holds promise for treating clinical populations with limited social and sequencing capacities (e.g., autism) with anodal tDCS.

candidates.title: Self-Referential Social Processing in Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder: Advancing Theoretical Precision and Clinical Insights with Model-Based Neuroscience
candidates.abstract: Background. Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) often misjudge whether social cues, like eye contact, are meant for them, which can fuel symptoms and functional impairment. These difficulties appear to stem from disruptions in how social information is dynamically processed (“evidence accumulation”). We used neurocognitive joint modeling to investigate which neural signals shape evidence accumulation during gaze perception and whether these brain-behavior links help explain disrupted self-referential social processing.Methods. Leveraging EEG data from N=99 SZ, BD, and healthy controls (HC) during a self-referential gaze perception task, we built joint drift-diffusion models characterizing how different trial-level EEG features translated to evidence accumulation and behavior. Joint models were compared against each other (and models using task-averaged EEG or behavior only) for their ability to predict task behavior and relevant clinical dimensions, including paranoia, functioning, and cognition. We examined whether the best-performing model differentiated patients and HC.Results. The best-performing joint model explained evidence accumulation through trial-level fluctuations—not task averages—in two neural signals: CPP and frontal midline theta, implicated in subjective deliberation/certainty and top-down modulation, respectively. Less reliable translation of trial-level CPP signals to evidence accumulation impaired gaze perception in SZ and BD. Mapping how trial-level theta dynamics translated to evidence accumulation captured paranoia and functioning better than behavior or task-averaged neural metrics alone.Conclusions. Model-based approaches that embrace the within-person variability of neural signals may reveal more nuanced, clinically relevant perspectives on the pathophysiology of SZ and BD than those using task-averaged brain activity or behavior alone.

candidates.title: Modeling decision dynamics disentangles working memory, cognitive control and reinforcement learning and reveals clinical differences
candidates.abstract: Various neurocognitive processes contribute to reinforcement learning (RL) and decision making, requiring careful task designs and computational modeling to disentangle them. People rely on capacity-limited working memory (WM) to rapidly and flexibly adapt behavior during learning, together with slower incremental RL processes that support robust long-term retention. The RLWM paradigm was developed to isolate these contributions by manipulating WM demands during learning. Empirical and computational advances support the separability of such processes, but only imperfectly, because a given choice can often equally be attributed to use of WM vs. RL. Here, we show that jointly modeling decision dynamics - accounting not only for choices but also response time distributions, together with hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation - improves the ability to disentangle separable learning and cognitive control processes. Despite added complexity, models with decision dynamics improved parameter recovery and yielded accurate out-of-sample prediction for choices in a held-out test phase after learning. In contrast, models fit only to choices produced an inflation of RL learning rates and failed the out-of-sample test. Moreover, joint modeling also revealed a novel neurocognitive process by which participants proactively widen decision boundaries to increase response caution under increased WM load. Applying our model to patients with schizophrenia revealed a deficit in proactive control mechanisms as well as slowed incremental RL, which were masked by previous choice-only models, while replicating previously established WM deficits. In summary, we show how joint modeling enables accurate, model-based and mechanism-oriented computational phenotyping of psychopathologies.

candidates.title: An LLM canary in the online data coalmine: Bayesian reasoning problems as a capability-gap test for LLM contamination in online samples
candidates.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) by participants in online studies threatens the validity of behavioral research data. I propose that Bayesian reasoning problems, which have decades of well-replicated human performance benchmarks, can serve as calibrated detectors of LLM contamination in online samples - an approach I call a capability-gap test. In two preregistered pilots of a Bayesian reasoning training tool (N = 148), participants' accuracy on positive predictive value (PPV) calculation problems reached roughly three times established human performance ceilings. Specifically, 57% of Pilot 2 participants achieved perfect 5/5 scores, against a meta-analytic ceiling of approximately 24% for a single problem presented in natural frequency format, a level at which perfect scores are effectively unattainable. Including two outcome measures - accuracy (correct numerical answer) and Bayesian algorithm use (evidence of the reasoning process) - allows researchers to distinguish LLM contamination from authentic learning effects: accuracy detects contamination, while algorithm use preserves treatment effect signals. This is itself a signal detection problem, structurally analogous to the mass screenings for low-prevalence problems around which the Bayesian reasoning literature was developed. Bayesian reasoning problems offer four advantages as contamination detectors: well-established human performance ceilings from meta-analyses, a large human-LLM performance gap, known reference distributions enabling nuanced assessment, and ease of embedding in existing surveys. I provide practical recommendations for using these problems as data quality diagnostics in online research.

candidates.title: The Evolution of Financial Time Series Forecasting: From Classical Econometrics to Temporal Foundation Models and Multimodal LLMs
candidates.abstract: Financial time series forecasting sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, econometrics, and machine learning. The data generating processes involved are characterized by non-stationarity, regime-dependent volatility clustering, very low signal-to-noise ratios, and reflexive feedback between market participants and asset prices. Over roughly six decades, the dominant methodology has moved through five recognizable phases: classical linear econometrics (ARMA, ARIMA, regularized VAR, VECM), conditional volatility modeling (ARCH/GARCH families, Stochastic Volatility), recursive online signal processing (LMS, RLS, Kalman filters), deep sequence learning (LSTMs, TCNs, patch-based Transformers, State Space Models), and the contemporary period (2024--2026) of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), Temporal Language Models (TLMs), and LLMs adapted for financial reasoning. For the purposes of the comparative analysis in Section~10, the deep learning phase is split into two paradigms (recurrent/convolutional networks and Transformer-based architectures), and the foundation model phase is similarly split into numerical TSFMs and multimodal LLM adapters, yielding seven paradigm entries in total. This paper traces that trajectory through the lens of what we call the Capacity-Adaptability Trilemma, a three-way tension between representational capacity, online adaptability, and structural interpretability. We also examine where foundation models fall short in financial contexts, documenting how benchmark contamination and architectural mismatches can cause large zero-shot models to underperform simple statistical baselines. To address this, we propose Econometrically-Informed Neural Networks (EINNs) as a way to embed econometric constraints into modern deep architectures. We present four self-contained synthetic experiments conducted on a MacBook Air M1. These provide limited empirical illustration of several paper claims: that model class rankings shift with SNR and nonlinearity structure (consistent with the trilemma framing), that a noise-dependent crossover exists between DLinear and PatchTST, that trained autoregressors do not beat naive persistence on synthetic random walks, and that the proposed VECM regularizer improves spread stationarity in a bivariate cointegrated setup.

candidates.title: Idiographic Memory Modelling in ACT-R Using Alternating Maximum Likelihood Estimation
candidates.abstract: Abstract Performance on memory tasks varies systematically between individuals and within individuals over time. However, computational models of memory are often fitted at the group level or summarise performance in a single parameter, potentially obscuring the distinct cognitive processes that give rise to this variation. Here we present a likelihood-based procedure for fitting the multi-parameter ACT-R declarative memory model at the level of the individual. Using this method, we jointly estimate five participant-level or idiographic parameters, each capturing a distinct component of memory performance, together with item-level variation in memorability. A parameter recovery study on synthetic data shows that these participant- and item-level parameters are jointly identifiable from realistic amounts of data on a typical spaced repetition memory task, requiring only about 40–90 observations of response accuracy and speed per participant. We demonstrate the method on a dataset of individuals with mild cognitive impairment and age-matched healthy controls, finding that mild cognitive impairment is marked by differences in three parameters signifying accelerated forgetting, less efficient memory retrieval, and general psychomotor slowing. These results show that the method can successfully decompose observed performance on a memory task into separable, individually interpretable components. More broadly, this work contributes to the development of fine-grained idiographic memory models that can capture dynamics in memory performance both between and within individuals, with applications in experimental research and applied settings, such as computational phenotyping for clinical diagnosis.

candidates.title: Negativity Bias in Person Perception: Exploring the Reverse Side of the ‘What Is Beautiful Is Good’ Stereotype in Women
candidates.abstract: According to the attractiveness halo effect, global person perceptions are biased by physical attractiveness. Few studies have shown similar influences by unattractiveness, with unattractive people being ascribed negative attributes. This preregistered study compared the strength of (positive) attractiveness halo effects with negative halo effects employing target samples from two phenotypically distinct populations. Facial photos of 154 German and 149 Brazilian women were judged separately for their attractiveness, social (in-)competence, intellectual (in-)competence, and emotional (in-)stability by 168 female German raters. Results showed moderate-to-strong positive associations of perceived attractiveness with all three positively framed attributes, and moderate-to-strong negative correlations with all three negatively framed attributes, with the latter negative halo effects being stronger than (positive) attractiveness halo effects only in some cases. Negative halo effects were stronger for Brazilian compared to German targets. In exploratory analyses, judgements of social competence, intellectual competence, and emotional stability were in most cases significantly more negative for low- than for medium-attractiveness targets, than they were positive for high- than for medium-attractiveness targets. These findings provide a systematic comparison of positive and negative halo effects, revealing that negative biases for unattractive individuals can be at least as pronounced as positive biases for attractive individuals. These effects also mostly generalise across German and Brazilian faces, extending evidence on halo effects beyond single-population samples.

candidates.title: Evaluating the Generation and Detection of Arabic-Based Phishing Attacks Using LLMs
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Phishing remains the most prevalent form of cybercrime globally, and large language models (LLMs) have removed the human-authorship constraint that historically limited its scale and sophistication. Arabic-language phishing has received comparatively limited empirical attention to date, despite the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region's exposure to cyber-attacks and Arabic's distinct morphology, script, and cultural communication norms. This study presents an empirical evaluation of LLM-based generation and detection of Arabic-language phishing emails. Three LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude and Falcon AI) generated a dataset of 290 Arabic email scenarios. Detection was evaluated using three LLM classifiers (Gemini, DeepSeek and Mistral) and 45 human participants, with both evaluator groups providing written justifications for thematic analysis. All three generating models produced convincing Arabic phishing content, each exhibiting a distinct social engineering strategy; Falcon AI's Gulf-specific institutional framing proved hardest for humans to detect despite its smaller parameter count. LLM-based detection substantially outperformed human detection: Gemini achieved 100% accuracy, DeepSeek 96.6%, and Mistral 66.9%, against a human mean accuracy of 68.0% (SD = 17.3%), with more than one in five LLM-generated phishing emails evading human recognition. Reasoning analysis revealed that LLM evaluators relied on categorical indicators while human participants depended on sender-address scrutiny, exposing a structural detection blind spot. These findings offer the first empirical evidence on Arabic-language LLM-driven phishing and inform culturally grounded cybersecurity defenses for the Gulf region.

candidates.title: Do we carry the false belief that LLMs have a theory of mind?
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) match and even exceed human-level performance across a battery of Theory of Mind (ToM) assessments. This has led to speculation that LLMs possess ToM capabilities. In this study, we test this claim by using the Unexpected Transfer task (i.e., the Sally-Anne test) to assess five up-to-date LLMs. The results indicate that while each model cumulatively performed above chance, they regularly defaulted to using less costly heuristics in place of dynamically tracking mental states. Most task failures resulted from an inability to integrate causality and “common-sense” pragmatic inferences into their reasoning processes. These findings suggest that LLMs have yet to develop robust ToM capabilities, calling for a systematic review of the present association between LLMs and ToM.

candidates.title: Preprint: Observational learning of disgust responses
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: By drawing on the prior experiences of others rather than learning through one’s own experience, individuals can avoid threats associated with direct physical contact. Although observational learning of fear is well established, less is known about whether disgust can be acquired through observational learning and how persistent such socially acquired responses are during direct exposure. We developed a video-based observational disgust-learning paradigm in which 40 healthy participants observed a demonstrator displaying disgust in response to an aversive odor (observed unconditioned stimulus, obs US). The demonstrators’ disgust responses were preceded by a neutral visual cue (conditioned stimulus, CS+), whereas a second cue (CS-) was followed by no response from the demonstrator. Participants subsequently encountered the CS+ and CS- directly. Repeated-measures analyses revealed successful observational disgust learning, indicated by conditioned responses measured as subjective ratings, respiration, and facial expressions. In particular, the CS+ elicited greater unpleasantness, disgust, and expectancy of the US than the CS-. Furthermore, respiratory breath amplitude decreased selectively for the CS+, while facial expressions did not differentiate between the CS+ and CS-. During subsequent direct exposure, CS differentiation in the subjective measures persisted and facial expression analysis revealed greater activation of the upper lip raiser for the CS+ than the CS-. These findings demonstrate that disgust responses can be acquired through observation alone and shape the observer’s responses when encountering cues that previously predicted others’ disgust responses. Our results reveal how social learning contributes to affective and bodily responses of disgust.

candidates.title: Reciprocal relationships between social support and depression among military cadets in Taiwan: findings from a long-term cross-lagged panel analysis
candidates.abstract: IntroductionThis study examines the reciprocal relationship between social support and depressive symptoms among military cadets in Taiwan, a population facing unique academic and military pressures. While emerging adults are prone to mental health challenges, they encounter additional stressors such as strict hierarchies and separation from family. Social support is known to be a protective factor, yet its long-term effects and bidirectional relationship with depression remain underexplored, particularly in collectivist military cultures where mental health may be stigmatised. Using a cross-lagged panel model with three waves of data, this study also explores whether this relationship varies by gender.MethodsA secondary analysis of longitudinal data was conducted from the "Career Development of Military Academy Students" project, which surveyed all Taiwanese military academy students from the 111th class across three waves (W1-W3). The final sample consisted of 898 students (73.2% male, average age=20.9) from six military academies. To analyse the bidirectional relationship between social support and depression, autoregressive cross-lagged panel analysis using structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed. Multigroup SEM was used to assess gender difference.ResultsThe cross-lagged panel model revealed reciprocal effects between social support and depression in the overall sample, evident only between W1 and W2. From W2 to W3, depression influenced perceived social support, with a stronger effect observed in males than females. These results underscore the unique dynamics of social support and depression in military contexts, particularly for females, where the relationship appears more complex.ConclusionsThe findings highlight the need for both systemic support structures and individualised interventions in military settings, considering gender differences and the evolving nature of mental health challenges. By addressing these factors, military leaders and mental health professionals can better support cadets in managing stress and depression, fostering a more resilient and mentally healthy military community.

candidates.title: [Exploring the Entrustment Decision Experiences of Preceptors Regarding New Nurses' Independent Patient Care]
candidates.abstract: BackgroundWithin the framework of competency-based medical education, determining whether new nurses are capable of making patient care decisions independently is a critical issue in clinical nursing education. However, there is a lack of in-depth exploration of clinical preceptor experiences related to entrustment decision-making in this context.PurposeThis study was designed to explore the experiences of nursing preceptors in terms of developing the confidence necessary in new nurses to make independent clinical decisions during the preceptorship process.MethodsA qualitative research design was employed. Using purposive sampling, eighteen nursing preceptors with experience mentoring new nurses were recruited. Semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted between August 2020 and July 2022. All of the interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analyzed using categorical-content analysis, and iterative discussions were conducted among research team members to ensure analytical rigor.ResultsFive major themes were identified: (1) observation and verbal confirmation of independent care competence; (2) incorporating feedback from the healthcare team as supportive evidence for decision-making; (3) adjusting the frequency of supervision based on task characteristics; (4) granting apparent entrustment while maintaining indirect supervision; and (5) limited nursing competence in adapting to changing clinical situations.ConclusionsClinical preceptors' trust in new nurses is established through a gradual and dynamic entrustment decision-making process that integrates clinical observation, task-related risk assessment, and team feedback. The findings of this study may serve as a reference for the development of clinical teaching, supervision, and entrustment strategies in nursing education.

candidates.title: A mixed methods evaluation of a six-year primary care community safety net-academic partnership model
candidates.abstract: To expand the tripartite mission to advance health equity, academic medical centers (AMCs) need to look outside their walls. In 2018, Stanford's primary care division launched the Community Partnership Program (CPP) between their AMC and local safety-net community health centers (CHCs) to support the goals of meaningful community engagement and addressing local clinic capacity needs. The CPP embeds Stanford physician faculty in local CHCs through service agreements. This study aimed to characterize the experiences of CHC leaders and faculty involved in the CPP to better understand barriers and facilitators to program implementation and assess its success as a community-responsive partnership. Stanford's CPP faculty (n = 9/15) and representative CHC leadership (n = 9/11) from 5 partner CHCs participated in the study. The National Academy of Medicine's Assessing Community Engagement Conceptual Model guided an explanatory mixed methods study: cross-sectional survey followed by semistructured interviews. A modified Enage for Equity Community Engagement Survey identified high- and low-scoring variables (Likert scale: 1-strongly disagree/never to 5-strongly agree/always). Qualitative assessment explored facilitators and barriers to program implementation and success. Overwhelmingly, both CHC leaders and faculty (n = 18) highlighted the CPP's positive role in making their work meaningful (4.78 [0.5]) and trusting the partners they work with (4.50 [0.5]). Sufficient time (3.61 [1.0]) and financial support (3.33 [1.4]) to engage in the CPP were the lowest scoring variables. Qualitative results highlighted the importance of communication, trust, and institutional buy-in, the value of community-academic bridges, increased access to clinical care, development of community-aligned solutions, and the partnership's positive impact on well-being. A model of community-academic partnership with primary care faculty embedded in safety-net CHCs can be successful from both AMC and CHC perspectives. These findings offer pragmatic lessons that can support other AMCs in building their own capacity for equity-focused collaboration grounded in community-engaged principles.

candidates.title: Evaluating Sycophancy in Chinese Large Language Models on Factual Questions Derived from Online Search Queries
candidates.abstract: As large language models increasingly mediate information access, factually accurate and independent answers are critical. However, these models can exhibit sycophancy by aligning their responses with users' stated beliefs even when those beliefs are incorrect, potentially presenting misinformation as independently verified and reinforcing users' confidence in false claims. Prior work leaves unresolved whether introducing user beliefs causes correct responses to become incorrect or uncertain, or causes uncertain responses to become belief-aligned incorrect answers. It also remains unclear whether anti-sycophancy interventions preserve or restore factual accuracy or merely shift responses toward uncertainty. We analyze factual sycophancy in Chinese-language information seeking using yes/no fact-checking questions. Our analysis covers 364,941 responses from three frontier Chinese-based LLMs (DeepSeek, Qwen, and Doubao) to 12,165 factual questions derived from real-world Chinese search queries. We evaluate the models with and without reasoning across baseline, belief-conditioned, and anti-sycophancy prompting, tracing matched shifts among correct, incorrect, and uncertain responses. Under incorrect user beliefs, we distinguish belief-aligned errors from losses of factual confidence, in which initially correct answers become uncertain. Patterns vary across models and reasoning settings: reasoning is not a consistent safeguard, and anti-sycophancy instructions can reduce incorrect agreement while increasing uncertainty. In Chinese-language factual question answering, avoiding agreement with false beliefs is therefore not equivalent to preserving factual accuracy, highlighting the value of transition-level evaluation. Such behavior may undermine the reliability of LLM-mediated information access by reinforcing misinformation or weakening users' confidence in factually correct answers.

preprint_updates.title: When and why are social categories overused relative to individuating information? A Bayesian approach to identifying biases in impression formation processes
